LEN ORE. Restless waves wers onward rolling, As in dreamy langour strolling, 3ne sad theme my thoughts controlling, I explored the sea's dim shore. Ehadeful twilight fast descending. Day in night was swiftly ending; Ands prayer from me ascending Mingled with the ocean's roar,' For a maiden far, far distant Wh)m I might not see once more— Said the ocean, "Nevermore ! " O'er the daylight weak and faiFng I beheld the gloom prevailing, And its presence nature hailing As it deepened more and more. In my heart I felt all gladness Overcome by wistful sadness, For a pathos strong to madness On my helpless spirit bore. To my anguished cry arising, "Shall I see her evermore?"— Cried the oeean, "Nevermore I" • Row I marvelled at its boldness! Then a wave of chilling coldness Struck my heart with fears.that told less Of sweet hope than etchings sore. Strange! here in the sombre gloaming, With the dusky shadows roaming ily the waves now wildly foaming, I should learn that nevermore In this world of many chances I should meet the one of yore ! Wailed the ocean. " Nevermore ! " Still along the shore I wandered, Over shells profftsely squandered— Right and left my steps meandered • As uncertain f',9 before. Soon the winds were crying louder To the sea that shoreward bowed her— So the moonlight faintly showed her; Rushing madly to the shore! - To my ques• ion almost shrieking, Shrieking, '' Never, nevermore" Shall I meet her?—" Nevermore ! ' " Monster ! thing-of ceaseless motion; I defy thy crazy notlon " • I exclaimed in my slevction To the maiden I adore. "It is false ! I yet shall meet her, With earrerses gentleet greet her, With resistless words entreat her Not to leave me evermore! Not to leave sie, but, a blessing, Stay with me for evermore— Yelled the wean, " Nevermore !"

. Horror-stricken, round me glaring, At the ocean mutely staring, Savage at its tone so daring, At its pror hecy so sore; with paesi-nate repulsion, And a siekening convulsion. Wished my soul its quick expulsion From a body I abhor; Such a state, so lone and dreary, I would quit for evermore.— Moaned the ocean,' Nevermore!" I felt despair within me, latent, • De pair around nis sadly patent, And in the ocean's voice so blatant, Heard the everlasting roar Which urged despair in tones inotific. And ah ! Despair, my soul's specific, Struck my heart with fears terrific, Pierced it to the very care; Stopped its beating—was ,t sinful ? Stopped, I prased, for evermore— Said the ocean, " Nevermore ! " "What, what is this?" I cried, as wheeling Round all frightened, my senses reeling, I saw huge shadows grimly stealing On te hid to those before! Then the waves apeared to mock me, Wildly rush, as it to kiceck me; How their anger seemed to shock are, For I scampe ed on and o'er. Never looking, r nly hearing What I Icath-s1 for evermore.— Ocean's erusl " Nevermore ! " • But swiftly followed my tormentor, - . As on some horrid errand sent. for I caught the acoents of the stentor Demon of this frightful shore Echoed in the hollows (rock riven ' • By seas that ers-, in fury driven, Had he-cn, and to the Naiads given ee: The cave:ns for evermore). These echoes filicl each horifice, then Dwindled to a whispered roar, Repeating "Never, ne.-ermore ! Pausing, tortured by the racking Thoughts my fevered mind attacking By the voice for ever tracking Me, wi- o fled with heart so sore. Peering at the eriffs kigh reaching, - On whose shelve:, the sea-birds sareeching, • Mimic T iel the ocean's teaching, Aye, by throats a thousand score, That eternal g ief remained me, For the one whose face once wore Smiles which haunt ma evermore. Listening,. while all hope receding Left me to the bitter pleading 01 a heart on anguish feediag— On thy memory, Lenore ! • Trembling, as the recAlectien' . • Of thy face's strange perfection • - - Swept across ties weird complexion 01 thii devil-ridden sh re, Rousing life, and light, and beauty, In the attitude they bore, Once by thee—my lost Lenoie ! Was the darkness growing deeper? Was the great cliff getting steeper? Had th- se:s designed to sweep her From my sight—my sweet Lenore? Surely night was never drearer ! Sureiy death was never nearer Ti myself, the living, hearer mad sea's prsphetic roar! For thervision sped, and lett me Grovelling upon the shore; Groaned the eczaa "Evermere !" Long beside the cliffs I've waited, Like a wanderer ill-fated, Or some traveler belated On a tempest-stricken shore. Still the hateful billows crash on; Still I feel the old, old passion : I Would that God would fashion Me a rock, or stoop to pour Lethean mercies oe my head! But no! I wait for thee, Lenore! Alas! that murmur s• Nevermore !" Warrington, December, 1832. " DRYS. BAISDON.

PIGEOYS.—THE EYE OF THE HORNER.—It is an in- teresting thing at all times to steely the eye of any living thing, whether human or not, and old pigeon fanciers pay a great deal of attention to this important part of the birds in. selecting them. The eye of man is not very unlike that of a pigeon, with this difference, however, that the latter hive, in addition to the two eyelids which we poesese, a third which is placed in the inner side of each eye. This meta- brine is transparent, and moves horizontally across the eye, serving as a protection to it. A depression or flattening of the cornea—that pert of the eye forming the outer cover- log of the pupil immediately in front, would, independently of any alteration of the crystaline lens, necessarily have the effect of extending the length of the focus, or, in other words, would lengthen the sight. It is probable, therefore, that this third or inner membrane performs in feathered creation another function beyond the purely mechanical one of cleaning the eye—preserving it from the action of the winds, or strength of the sun's rays, which are usually ascribel to it—namely, that of assisting to lessen the con- vexity of the cornee, and thus giving the birds further range and acuteness of vision superior to ;animels. Then, again, it may be that the iris, which is the circular coloured portion surrounding the pupil, plays another :part than that of merely controlling the amount of light admitted to the retina. It has often been noticed in birds which have proved themselves swift and long flyers that there is a strong con- tractive and expansive action of the iris, and it is this which gives he appearance of wild or fire so often spoken of by morning pigeon fanciers. The colour of the eye varies in manv different varieties, but it is a strange fact that nearly all the best birds have blue or light-coloured eyes, and this has also been noticed, not only with birds o' pray, bat also it is a peculiar thing that nearly all the beet shots at Wimbledon are men with light-coloured eyes. Much of what we have stated is theoretical, as the question has never been decisively settled, but it certainly has much to 1 support it. RABBITS.—THE DIITCH.—This is one of the smallest of rabbits, but it is a very valuable' variety, being both pretty and useful. Dutch are about the most prolific of all the rabbit tribe, which is certainly saying a great deal. They have not quite such large litters as some others, five to seven-being average numbers, but are remarkable for bring- ing up their young ones with little if any loss. They are very hardy, but do best at a uniform temperature and in- doors. Does of this breed are very often used as nurses for other and more tender varieties, and for this purpose they are capital; but we =not approve of the plan of depriving them of their litter, when half-grown, and giving them another litter of very young ones, thus making them do doable duty. This is a very risky practice, and is certain in time to undermine the health of the animals. A mistake Is made by many fanciers in trying to get very small speci- mens of this variety, and we think too much is made of diminutive size, as in order to obtain it inbreeding and other questionable practices are often resorted to ; five or six pounds weight Is about right, and whilst we are quite aware that very large specimens get coarse and lose much of theirteauty, yet it is a great pity to go to the other extreme. The colours which We find amongst Dutch are black, blue, gray, fawn, yellow, silver gray, tortoise-shell, or lemon is the ground colours, but the moat important thing is that the markings shall be regular, and distinct. The markings generally adopted are that the 15ind feet shall be tipped with white, and the saddle of the ground colour. The whole of the forelegs are white, and a band of white runs over the shoulders, thus enveloping the legs in a wide collar of white. This collar should be very cleanly marked, and the edge of it be very straight and distinct. The head is of the gr end colour, with a thin streak of white called a blaze, coming down the face and covering the nose. The ears mutt stand upright, and any tendency to lopping or falling over is regarded with very great objection. They are only moderately long, the very objection just named preventieg any development of them The great difficulty in breeding Dutch is to get all the markings clearly defined and distinct, as there is always a tendency to one colour running into another, and where this is the case it is fatal to any chance in the show-pen. • Those who do not show need not be so particular, though probably the desire to have really good specimens will make them reject each as are wanting in the qualities we have mentioned. HEATING PIGEON LOFTS AND ATIAUTEs.—The heating of pigeon houses and aviaries at the present time of the year is a most important matter, and it is 'in most cases a most necessary thing to do, but requires to be pro- perly managed or more harm than good will be done. It the pigeon loft is adjoining a warm and substantial building, and only the hardier varieties are kept, then artificial heat may be dispensed with, but otherwise, or in aviaries, than it must be provided, as delicate cage-birds cannot stand the rigours of our climate. The greatest danger is in heating the loft or aviary too much, as then the birds are made tender and cannot stand any sudden change. Open fires even when we'l protected are very troublesome as they re- quire frequent attention, and often the fire is great at one time and almost out at another. Gas or oil stoves are oh- jecti mable as they vitiate the atmosphere. The best thing We have seen for the purpose is a small stove, which burns anthracite coil or coke, celled "The Tortoise," and made by Messrs. C. Portway J.: Sons, of Halstead, Essex. This is portable, and is sold complete with several feet of piping to go through a wall or into a chimney, for 21s. 6d., and as it is easily managed and burns six to eight hours without attention, it is most suitable for such a purpose as we have tweed It will heat a large loft or aviary sufficiently to keep the inmates comfortable, and there can be no tainting of the atmosphere. An Irishman on board a vessel when she was on the point of fouudering, 'being desired to come on deck as she was going down, replied that he had no wish to go on deck to see himself drowned. .Magistrate: "You are charged with having emptied a basin of water over the plaintiff." Irishwoman: "Share, your honour, you must forgive me; in the dark I took the gentleman for my husbend." "Madame," he said, sorrowf ally, "I shill never be young again." "N e" she replied, regarding him with a cynical expression, when nature makes a mistake she never repeats the expriment with the same material." Mrs. Croeseatch was engaging a servant. " Ybu will find me rateer crose, sometimes," said she. "Och ! ma'am," ex- chimed Bridget, "I'm used to that. I never mind a cross mistress." Nor did she, as Mrs. C. found after she had en- gaged her. "No, sir!" slid Dr. Jalap ; "I wouldn't have that apple tree cut down for money." "But you never get any fruit from it," argued Brown; "the boys steal all the apples before they are half ripe." " That's jest it," replied the doctor with a quiet smile. "That tree stands me in a good £5O a year." When Sir George Rose Was dining on one occasion with the late Lord Langdale, his host s.peke of the very diminu- tive church in Langdale, of which his lordship was patron. "It is not bigger," said Lord Langdale, "than this dining- room." "No," returned Sir George, "and the living not half so good." The wife of a Parisian, _returning home, rang at her own door. Nobody coming, she rang again. Still nobody ap- peared. Finally, at a loader and longer ring, the man=ser- vant concluded to show himself. "Pray, are you deaf ?" said the lady. "I tog your pardon, madam," said he, tran- quilly, "bat I heard only the third ring." Sir Fletcher Norton, whose want of courtesy was note- none, happened, while pleading before Lord Mansfield on Some question of manorial right, to say, "My Lord, I can illustrate the point in an instant in my own person. I my- self have two little manors." "We all know it, Sir Fletcher," the Judge interposed, with one of his blandest smiles. Augustus was told of an extravagant Roman knight who had wasted all his property. When his goods were sold by auction, Augustus commissioned a person- to bid for his pillow. Being asked why he wished to have this article of furniture in particll4r, he replied, "Such a pillow must be very desirable neon which a man so deep in debt could sleep So Soundly., Not long after his removal from the House of Commons to the House of Lords, Disraeli met a brother Peer in the street, who asked him how he liked the change. "Like it," exclaimed Disraeli, forgetting himself for the moment, and blundering out the truth, " L.ika it ! I feel as if I were dead, or buried alive !" Then, seeing the expression of discomfi- ture on the Peer's face, he added hastily, with a courtly bow and an irresistible smile," And in the land of the blessed !" A CILI2IOIIS TAsTg.—The Malagasy taste for tomb-build• ing was another frequent cause of delay. Among the Heva, large sums are spent on their tombs, which are a kind of vault, made of immense slabs of undressed blue basalt rock. / A man will live in a house which has not cot more than from ten to twenty dollars, but he will cheerfully expend 200 or 300 dollars upon his tomb. As soon as a young man marries and settles in lila he begins preparations for build- ing his family vault; and all his spare time and most of his spare money are spent upon this work. The basalt slabs are of.en brought for two or three miles' distance, dragged by hundreds of neople, all the family connections and friende going to midst. Although the portions underground in these tombs are o/ undressed stone, above ground a massive, and often elaborate structure of drtssed stone is erected, with bold mouldings, and sometimes with a good deal of carving.—From "The Quiver" for December. ADVERTISING.—Many of the advertisements of American papers are characterised by rough and ready humour. Who has not heard of the attractive announcement by a large iholstery firm :—" Their parlour furniture is elegant; their bedroom furniture is rich; their mattresses are downy; their coffins are comfortable!" And equally well-known is the advertisement of a Pennsylvania grocer, who inscribed, In white letters, on the fence of a graveyard, "Use Jones's bottled ale if you would keep out here." For skill in paint- ing the lily and adorning the rose no one has ever excelled the wideawake American trader. Nothing could go beyond the advertisement I met with lately of a Yankee auctioneer. It offered for sale a "sweet and pensive retirement" on the banks of the Hudson, and after describing the "streams of sparkling brightness," and the "fruits of the tropics in golden beauty," mentions that "the stables are worthy of the steeds of Nimrod or the studs of Achilles, and its heronry was built expressively for the birds of Paradise, while sombre In the distance, like the cave of a hermit, glimpses are caught of the doghowe." AN ENRAGED PEfILISTINE.—The fact is, I am sick and tired of culture. My own wife and daughters have got it in the most virulent form, and they have introduced it into every room of my house, and into every shelf in my library. They have taken my own sanctum of sanctums in hand, and they have reitheticised it for me from floor to ceiling against my will. But all that I could overlook: what I can't over- look is their gibes and jeers at me for being a Philistine. Now, why shouldn't I be a Philistine in my own quiet un- obtrusive way, if only I choose to be so? I don't go about interfering with persons of culture, and why should persons of culture interfere with me? I let them enjoy their blue china by their own oyermantels ; I let them read their old French ballades in their Chippendale arm-chairs; I let them discuss Fra Angelico or Fra Diavolo, whichever they please, without a word of blame or remonstrance; and why, in the name of all that's sacred, can't they let me repose in peace at Askelon Villa, Gath, without dragging me forth per- petually from my gentle retirement to point their moral and adorn their tale? Do I ever throw stones at their adored Aphrodite; and if not, why should they throw stones at my peaceful and unobtrusive Dagon ? They may not happen to admire his fishy tail and his general siunousness and suppleness of outline; but neither do I admire the brazen- faced demeanour and extremely scanty attire of their Cytherean hussy. What I ask is Ibis: May not a quiet sugar-broker's cler.k of a Philistine like myself enjoy life after his own fashion without being held up to ridicule daily In a philmsthetic Press, as the incarnation of all that is stolid, stupid, lose, and Tulgar la our poor Won human naurelgralrUt

dreamt that I, a barrister, wi an income from property of £l,lOO a year, would ever become, from choice, a common tramp, known among not a few of the fraternity as" Carroty Joe," and credited With being an "A 1 mumper." My home was in a village on the coast of North Devon, and as a bachelor, without near relatives, not a few scheming mammas within a circle of half a dozen miles tried to hook me for one of their daughters. But I had formed an ideal, and none of the girls in the neighbourhood came up to it. I was getting fast on for thirty, and my friends began to re- gard me as a confirmed bachelor, when Lily Warren came on a visit to her uncle, at the village rectory, aril I was subdued at once. Lily was not what would generally be termed beautiful, not even pretty, for though her hair was golden, her eyes a lovely blue, and her complexion purity itself, her features were irregular, and her nose decidedly Oetrousse. But her nobleness of soul shone out in her countenance; here at last was my ideal. In a few days we had beco:ne fast friends and the rector and his lady were quite content. Lily's father was dead, and her mother an invalid, a married sister being her only other near relative ; and the rector knew it would take a load of care from her mother if Lily was comfortably settled in life. The course of true love ran smooth enough for a few weeks, and then an event took place which threatened to wreck the hopes I bad been cherishing, and to turn my happiness into misery. Lily's sister Ethel had not been well since the birth of her second child, and the doctors ordered her to France. Ethel's husband, a country squire, wished to leave their son and heir with the rector, but Lily insisted on the little boy being left in her charge. He was a handsome little chap, a miniature copy of Lily, his long golden curls making him look quite girlish. He soon grew attached to me, probably as the result of various mechanical toys I procured for him from London. One day when the heat of the June sun was slightly tempered by the fleecy clouds that'slowly floated overhead, Lily and Bertie set out for a walk, and as was my wont, I joined them as they passed my lodge gate. For a while we sauntered slowly along, until, the sun having broke through the clouds, the-heat became oppressive, and we turned into the park. " Under a spreading chesnut tree," we sat down, and soon became absorbed in a book—" Childe Harold," so absorbed indeed, that we did not miss bertie, who had run into the road after a butterfly. But after a while, I felt Lily shiver, and proposed returning home—but where was Bertie? I called him, but to no purpose, and we hurried home as quickly as possible, hoping he had safely arrived there. But he had not been seen. and Lily was over- whelmed with grief. The whole neighbourhood was ap- prised of his absence, and men, women, and children were soon scouring the country round. The police were informed, the telegraph set to work, and all through the night the search was kept up, but without success—no tidings what- ever could he gleaned of the missing child. A man and woman, apparently ordinary tramps, had been seen begging in the village, and their description was sent to all the towna within a hundred miles, but nothing came of it. As the days went by, and no news of Bertie came to hand, Lily was plainly suffering from the effects of grief. She blamed herself for allowing him to go out of her sight, and naturally could not bear the sight of me. I tried to think of some scheme which should put an end to her grief, and at the same time make us friends again. After much cogitation I resolved .rack the tramping couple; and In order the better tr accomplish my design, to turn tramp myself. I said nothing to Lily—in fact, she would not see me; but I wrote to her, telling her I would bring back Bertie, or never come home again. The couple I intended to track had gone in a wes- terly direction—probably into Cornwall, and thither I went. At Launceston I bought a seedy snit of Scotch tweed, and haring allowed my beard to grow, soon passed muster as a tramp. Finding that my ignorance of vagrant life and of lodging-house usages made me an object of suspicion, I picked up "Jack " as a companion, professing that I merely wanted a guide, aril that I would find us both in lodgings, grub, and 'bacca, an arrangement which suited Jack, as he said, "to a T." He showed nee all the "cribs" good for a "cant of vrittles," a" bob," or a " sprat ; "and as I went up to the houses and asked for work, telling him on my return I had " copped " a shilling or half a crown, he was full of my praises as an "out-an'-out good cadger." Sometimes I thought he suspected me; he could never understand why I always wanted to peep into all the lodging-houses in a town, before I mad dup my mind where to stay. But he fared too well, and had too easy a life, to trouble himself very much about it. I had been five months on tramp, and was apparently not a whit nearer the fruition of my hopes. We had tramped all over the south-western counties, and then made for London. I heard, however, in a well-known lodging-house in the borough, that the man I was seeking was known as "Jimmy the Needles," and that he never came to London, nor its immediate vicinity. Whilst I was deliberating which way to go next, Jack happened to wonder how many of my old pals 'would be at Swindon, on Christmas Day, helping the old German to eat his Christmas dinner. I guessed at once that it was _very probable "Jimmy the Needles would turn up there, and, much to Jack's disgust, at once resolved to' get there before Christmas Day. We travelled hard, and Jack, whose boots were not fit for long tramps, was done up. But his fears of losing me pre- ponderated over his desire to " skipper " for the night, and try to sneak in at the old German's in the morning, as he more than once proposed, and we pushed on as fast as he could go. Suddenly he gave vent to a series of expletives, and I saw we must give up all hope of reaching Swindon that night, for Jack had stepped on a large flint, and his big toe, which was outside his apology for a boot, had been severely cut. "That's horribly unlucky," said Jack, "for I'm thinking there'll be a big snowstorm to-night, and the snow may be too deep to go on to-morrow." The air had suddenly got terribly cold, and right glad WAS I when we had crept quietly into a barn, and climbed into the bay loft, where we buried ourselves in the hay, and munched the last big " cant " of bread and cheese I had obtained from the good natured wife of a farmer. When we awoke in the morning there was a foot of snow on the ground, and Jack demurred to going on. But the calls of his stomach proved stronger than his desire to rest his bad foot, and we reached Swindon comparatively early. The snow had made the old German more than usually benevolent, and after a little demur, and the assurance we should stay there two or three days, he let us in. There were about 70 lodgers—men, women, and chilren of all lages and descriptions. The kitchen into which Jack , ushered me was a very large one, but far too small for the number in it that morning. Jack was, "Hail fellow well met," with most of the motley crew, and introduced me to some of his oldest pals and acquaintances. As my eye wandered round the kitchen, it lighted upon one man, and pointing him out to Jack I asked who the man was. "Don't know the cave, but I'll ask the deputy ;" and he crossed over to where that worthy was replenishing the huge fire. I was right—it was "Jemmy the Needles ; " but what had become of the woman and the missing child? I dare not make inquiries, for I had no means of proving my story if I called in the aid of the police. I could only wait; but I determined not to lose sight of the man I had tracked at last. "There's going to be a wedding here presently," whispered a superannuated knife-grinder to me, "I hope the bloke will stand a few gallons of hot lush." I professed to be greatly interested in the affair, and was informed that a brush hawker, "fifty, if he was a day," hed. fallen in love, or said he had, with a good looking girl about nineteen, a cane chair mender; and dazzled by his promises that he would keep her at home like a lady, and not ask her to go out and sell, she had agreed to marry him that day by "jumping over the broomstick." And a curious ceremony it was. A ballad singer, or, in lodging lingo, a griddler, offered his services as parser), one of the landlord's white shirts doing duty as a surplice. A space having with much difficulty been cleared opposite the hearthstone, the bride and bridegroom marched in amid the shouts and jokes of the room full of lodgers. It was plainly to be seen that both had been primed for the occasion, for the bridegroom was noisy, and bade the parson "look sharp with your tom- foolery," whilst the face of the bride was aglow with sun- dry nips of gin, which some of the female hawkers in the house had given her to keep the cold out." A travesty of the marriage service was read out of an old Prayer Book, the aim of the " parson " being to excite the mirth of the company as much as possible, and the ceremony ended by the couple, hand-in-hand, jumping over a broomstick, held about a foot from the floor by two of the company. Tha bridegroom was pronounc%l regular jannocky bloke," for he had provided an eighteen gallon cask of beer, and a gallon of gin for the ladies. The landlord, howeTer,

would not allow either to be touched till after dinner, so after the wedding was over, I had nothing to do but watch , the company. They were certainly a motley crew. The "griddling" fraternity were well represented,_ for travellers know that at Christmas time the singing •ol2'cild fashioned Christmas carols, _even if the singing is inbre like a costermonger's bawl than anything else, is surelo pay well. There was one set, consisting of six young men and two young women, who sang fairly well, and, judging by the com- parative decency of their clothing, were "doing a good thing." One of the young men played a German concertina in a manner which preyed his perfect mastery of the instrument. The old German would not allow the least work to be done on Christmas Day in the house, on pain of forfeiting the dinner of the delinquent, and no male lodger must go out" cadging" till after dinner. I was indebted to Jack for these particulars, who also told me the " lurk " [Anglice, occupation] of most of the lodgers. " There's a cove," said be, pointing to a tall, rather good- looking man of about thirty, " who 'gammons' he's a broken-down-merchant, and he's got the gift of the gab so that he can make folks believe it. That chap with the bald hoed is a thimble-rigger in the racing season, and he could easy save enough to keep him thro' the winter if he wasn't so fond of gin hot. Now I reckon he's on the down right,' getting his grub and doss the best way he can. Yon bloke in the corner with the calf-skin weskit is a mush faker [umbrella mender], but his donor' [wife or female travel- ling companion] tells fortunes, and so be don't work much. That young fellow with the cheese-cutter cap is Dodging Tommy;' he's got the name of being the best mumper on the road. And blest if there aint ' Mooching Sam;' wonder when he came back again. He's been doing seven stretch [years] for setting a hay stack on fire. Poor beggar got tired of the road, and did it o' purpose to get lagged. Wonder how he liked it ! It's turned his hair gr_y, what there is left of it, anyhow. He wanted me to go with him, but bad as the road is, give me my liberty. I'm not as fond of quod as some of 'em. See that frowsy old womaa in you corner ? That's the governess.' She kep a crois crib in the Dials, and used to train little gals to *'buz '[pick pockets]. But the coppers were put fly to her, and after two stretch in the 'steel' [Colbath fields] she left the smoke. Now she sells caps for a living—what a come ilown!"

7-1 was naturally much amused by Jack's running corn- ments on those present, but suddenly the door opened, and -a woman entered carrying a, little boy. Could that be Bertie ? The golden curls had been cut short, and darkened by some means or other, the face also had been altered in complexion, probably—for I had read of such things—by one of those decoctions known to the gipsies ; but the same blue eyes were there, not now full of laughing glee, as I haA been won't to see them, but full of tears, for Vie child was nearly starved with the intense cold. The woman made for the fire, and "Jimmy the Needles " did the same. Under pretence of warming myself I went over and stood beside

them. -" Well, and how did you get on, Nell ?" Jimmy inquired. "Oh ! Fairish. I was fetching the coppers fast enough; but this young brat begun to cry, and folks said I ought to be ashamed to keep him out in the cold. But I've got nine bob; not bad for two hours." ",Stop your row, you imp, or I'll make you," and the savage gave the child a slap. My temper was roused, and I was Pearly betraying myself, for I could not bear to see Lily's favourite beaten by such a scamp. "You scoundrel," I.said, "How dare you illtreat a child

that is not your own ?" "Who says it's not ?" he asked, with a dangerous gleam in his eye. "Mind your own biz, or it 'll be worse for you, young fellow." Jack same over and pulled me away,and some of the other men bade me beware of Jimmy, for he'd a devil of a temper, and was a terrible slog'ger. I could see that Jimmy was watching me, so, quickly making up my mind, I beckoned Jack outside, and confided to him the whole affair, promising him a hundred pounds as soon as Bertie , had been restored to his friends. "A hundred quid ! Gee wimming ! I allus thought you were n't a cadger! So you've been foolin' me all the time when you said you got bobs and halt-dollars at the cribs I sent you to? Well, never mind; you're not foolin' me about the coin, are you ? " I reassured him, and tell trig him to go in and keep an eye on the child and its captors. I set off to the railway station, but the Government had not then obtained the telegraphs, and no private messages could he sent that day. There was then no telegraph office in the town, for Swindon was not of so much importance as it is now a-dais. I did not want the affair to get into the hands ot the police, if it could be avoided; besides I had not a particle of proof to support my story, beyond the possession of more money than a tramp should possess, and this might render me au object of suspicion. There was thus nothing for it but to wait till the morrow, though I longed to transmit the pre- cious news to Lily, and bring the roses to her cheeks again. I returned to the lodging house, and found that dinner— the old German's freed Christmas dinner was being put on the table. _ _ _

"Just in time, young man! Another couple of minutes and the door would ha' been.shut," said the deputy with a grin. Huge joints of roast beiSflyotatoes, and cabbage ad lib. ;ere placed_on the long tables, the women,-children; and old men sitting-down first, there not being room for all. At a signal from the old German, the concertina chap struck up the " Old Hundreth," and led by one of the grithilers the Doxology was sung in a manner that showed most of the lodgers were familiar with both words and tune, many of them having probably learnt it in gaol. I had had many opportunities of seeing how much tramps could eat when they had the chance, but the appetites of the good people who dined that day at the expense of the good-hearted land- lord seemed very loth to be satisfied. When it came to our turn, and Jack sat down, I really thought lee would make himself ill. Fun and laughter were merrilly indulged in at the expense of some, who having asked for the third or fourth helping of the plum pudding which followed the first course, found themselves unable to finish it. THE MUSH-FAKER'S GHOST. Told by the Mush-Faker in the calf-skin "weskit." "I daresay many of you will laugh at Die, but when I've told my tale you can laugh, if you like. Most of you'll know the ruined farm-house not far from Holsworthy, down in Devonshire, leastways, them as has travelled that part of the couatry. Well, the barn is still air-tight, and many's the poor traveller as has put up there for the night. List winter, just after Christmas, I was on the mooch down there, having sold my tool kit at the end of a spree in Bristol. Tommy the Dumps was with me, and though it was a bitter winter we could not raise browns enough for doss and bacca both. It came on to snow when we was near the ruined house, and I proposed to skipper it there. But Tommy couldn't see it, he said; Cockney Ned had told him of seeing a ghost in the barn, and he wouldn't go. I knew if we went on to Holsworthv we should have to go to the workhouse, and you all know what a bad bloke there is there. I had 21 days for smashing his windows once, and d;d not want to face him again, so I let Tommy go on, and turned into the barn. When I got up in the loft I found that somebody had been good enough to put Some straw there since I was there before, and so I dossed comfortable enough. But some time in the night I woke up as cold as workhouse charity. The snow had stopped, and the moon shined in the open window, lighting up the old place like day. I looked round. What's that in the corner? My hair seemed to lift my fur cap right off my head, my blood froze, my I teeth were like as if they were all loose—ugh ! I was " frit- ' tened " nearly out of my wits! For in that corner there was a thing the like of which I don't want to see again—no, never no more. It was the figure of old Joe Price, the gipsy mush-faker, all dressed in white, and you know he's been dead this four years—died in Portland when he was doing, seven stretch for passing snide (bad coin). "You're mistaken, Joe is alive now; it was another Joe Price, a cousin of Joe the mush-faker, as died at Portland," said the deputy of the house. "Joe was here last Christ- mas, making his way down to Cornwall, and very likely he had a game with you. But what did you do when you saw the ghost ?" "Why, I dropped clean from the loft to the floor, and run as fast as my legs would carry me to Holsworthy, knocked up the bobby, and slept in the cells all the rest of the night Very likely it was !Joe himself, but what a confounded trick to play on a brother tradesman." There was a general hearty laugh at the mush-faker's expense, and when the mirth had subsided, a "dry-land sailor" stood up, and said he could spin a far better yarn than that, but the company must excuse all blunders' as he was not used to telling tales. With his back to the fire, having taken a huge quid out of his mouth, he proceeded to tell what he styled A REAL GHOST STORY. "Three years sines this winter I was travelling with an old sailor, a rum old cove. Our lay was to travel round the coast, walking as near high water mark as possible, and picking up whatever was worth anything. Now and then we come across a dead sailor, and had his clothes and some- times a tidy bit of coin in 'ern. Once when we was on the Cornish coast, we got nearly sixty quid off a sailor's body, and lived in clover on it for three months. Well, we was on the Welsh coast, not a great way from Holyhead. The folks could not speak English, and we didn't know how far we was from town to town. One night it seemed as if we'd have to turn inland and look for a skipper. But we'd heard of a wreck in that neighbourhood, and made sure of finding a body or two. Just as we were giving it up we come'd across one. It was too dark to see what he was like, but we stripped off his clothes, hid 'em between two haystacks in a field, and walked on to Amlwch to sleep. In the middle of the night Jack screamed out, and woke me up. Oh! dear. Such a sight at the foot of the bed! A young sailor chap, with a face as ghastly as death, pointing to old Jack with its finger. Next minute it was gone, and I found old Jack had gone off in a dead faint. When he come to, he says, 'Where is my boy? He was here just now.' I tried to laugh it off, but he lay wake the rest of the night, and could not eat any breakfast. We went and took the duds from their hiding place, and on searching the pockets Jack found he had robbed the body of his own son, for there were four discharges from ships in his son's name. We went back to look for the body, but a high tide early that morning had was Led it out to sea. Jack went off his chump,' and is now in the 'sylum. That's all." No one hazarded a remark after thin story, but a diminu- tive Lonelou 11,11- have been any age from fourteen to eighteen whispered to his mate just behind me, "We'll try that dead sailor gems when we get to the sea, oh, Sam?"

The Home Secretary and the Bishop of St. Albans have administered a well-deserved and cutting relitike to the Rev. C. E. Taunton, of St. John's, Harlow, for the dis- creditable and offensive manner in which that " reverend " gentleman lately obstructed the funeral of a Noncon- formist. MR. GLADSTONE AND THE LIVERPOOL ELECTION.—Mr. W. E. Gladstone has sent to Mr. R. D. Holt, of Liverpool. a letter on the result of the recent contest in that city. The Premier congratulates the victorious candidate, the Liberal Association, and especially Mr. Holt,, who has so long, in days off practical gloom and under so many rebuffs, stood without flinching in the front of the battle. div.head: I,:XAMINEII, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 23, 1882.
div.p: THE I,:XAMINEII, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 23, 1882.

NISCELLA.NEOUS. The Bishop of Manchester has refused to institute the Rev. H. Cowgill to the benefice vacated by the Rev. S. F. Green. . Mr. Robert Donnell, barrister, Irish North-east Circuit, 'was accidentally drowned, on 'Tuesday, in the canal at Dublin. Mr. Fawcett continues to make satisfactory progress, and now needs but rest and change of scene to reach complete recovery. The Very Rev. Dr. Close; late Dean of Carlisle, died en Sunday night at Penzance. He was born in 1797. In 1856 he succeeded the late Primate in the Deanery of Carlisle. Gunton Hall, near Norwich, the seat of Lord Suffield, was found to be on fire early on Monday morning. A consider- able portion of the building was destroyed, but a large quan- tity of furniture, pictures, and books were saved. The fire was caused by the ignition of timber in a fine. The Premier and Mrs. Gladstone and Mr. W. H. Gladstone, M.P., on Monday attended at Hawarden the funeral of an old retainer on the estate, a servant who had been employed at Hatarden Castle for over 40 years. Mrs. Gladstone placed a handsome wreath of flowers on the coffin. The funeral service was read by the Rev. S. Gladstone. Mr. Ross, M.P., speaking at a Volunteer meeting at Pen- zance, on Monday afternoon, said, though a member of the Ppposition, he was bound to admit, putting aside the poli- tical aspect of the war, that a large measure of praise wes due particularly to Mr. Childers and Lord Northbrook for the efficient administration of their departments. At the Liverpool County Court, on Monday, Mary Gilligan seed a master stevedore for £5OO compensation for the death of her husband, who lost his life through the falling of a gangway over the bald of a vessel which he was assisting to load. The jury gave a verdict for £75, to be appropriated between Mrs. Gilligan and her five children. On Saturday, the dead body of Martha Ann Hibbert, aged 14, was taken out of the Huddersfield Canal at Ashton- under-Lyne. She was employed as a weaver at one of the local mills, and on Tuesday she returned home and said that she had been told she must leave because her work was bad. In the evening ,she went out, and was not seen alive again. The braes question is now in a fair way for settlement. The tenant of Ben Lee has signed an agreement giving up the remainder of his lease, but reserving to himself the right of applying fer compensation from Lord MacDonald, and the issue now lies directly between his lordship and the crofters. If is understood that both parties are anxious for a settlement. MR. GLADSTONE'S VISIT TO MIDLOTHIA.N.—The Marquis of Tweeddale, the Earls of Aosebery, Aberdeen, Elgin, Stair, and IBreadalbane, Lords ?,Reay and Thurlow, and almost the whole of the Scotch Liberal members, have already intimated their intention of being present at the banquet which is to be given to Mr. Gladstone at Edinburgh on the 18th January, by the Scottish Liberal Club. All the avail- able tickets have been applied ior. EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY.—At the Whitehaven County Court, on Tuesday, a jury awarded the widow of a miner named Casson £lB4 compensation for the death of her hus- band, who was killed in Sir James Bain and Co.'s mines in September through a chain breaking aid allowing a large weight to fall down the pit upon Casson. The weight had been attached to an indicator to show the quantity of water in the pit, and the evidence showed that the chain was not in proper order at the time of the accident. Tun' Acreox BY MRS. WELDON.—The summons by Mrs. - Weldon against Mr. Jeffrey, chairman of the Birmingham Festival Committee, to recover damages for, her exclusion ' from the performances of Gounod's work at the last Festival, came on at the Birmingham County Court, on Tuesday. It was stated that the plaintiff had been induced to accept certain terms offered by the other side, and the case was therefore struck out. THE MALAGASY ENVOYS.—The envoys from Madagascar received at the Alexandra Hotel, on Monday afternoon, those members of the Madagascar Committee who are at present in town, it being thought desirable that the oppor- tunity should not be lost of as many of the latter as could find it convenient making the personal acquaintance of the representatives of the island in which they are so much interested. The meeting was more of a social than of a formal character. How To WEAR a HELMET.—A general order from the Commander-in-Chief contains a " wrinkle " specially meant, we should imagine, for the volunteers, and teem following purpose:—" The helmete or shakos are not to be worn on one side of the head, but are to be placed evenly on the men's heads, and brought well down on the forehead, with the chin strap under the chin. The chin strap may be fastened to the hook near the top of the helmet when the helmet is worn otherwise than on duty or on parade."— Court Journal. CHARGE OF FORGERY.—The Hanley borough magistrates on Tuesday, committed William Joseph Fox, ironmonger, Hanley (late secretary of the local Starr-Bowkett Building Society), for trial at Stafford Assizes on a charge of forging a signature to a cheque for £2O 10s., the property of Job Lea, a member of the society. It was alleged that Fox, whilst secretary of the society, gave Lea £lB for bis shares and then drew a cheque on the society in the names of Lea, without Lea's knowledge, for £24 10s., the full valise of the share, then forged Lea's signature to it, and, as alleged, appropriated the money. COLLAPSE OF A RAILWAY BRIDGE.—Near Ecclesfield Station, on the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Rail- way, between Sheffield and Barnsley, on Tuesday, a bridge about thirty feet high was rendered unsafe by the subsi- dence of part of the embankment. A large passenger train and an engine and brakevan had only passed over the bridge a few minutes when the subsidence became - so serious that all traffic had to be suspended for six hours whilst the structure was strengthened. Communication was th in restored on one line, and it is hoped to have the bridge in a ,safe condition and traffic resumed over both lines. MURDER IN ABERDEENSHIRE.—At Aberdeen, on Monday, three farm-servants, named Meldrunn Murray, and Cheyne, were committed for trial orpa charge of murdering a wonehn 80 years of age, named • Penny, residing in the parish of Tarves, Aberdeenshire. The three men, it is alleged, went to the cottage where the woman named resided with her daughter at one o'clock in the morning, dragged the old lady out of bed, threw her into the snow, trampled upon her, and assaulted the daughter so severely that she lies in a critical coedition. Mrs. Penny died from the effects of the injuries she received. FREEDOM OF GLASGOW CONTERRED ON MR. FORSTER.— Mr. Forster was on Monday afternoon presented, at a large and influential meeting in the City Hall, Glasgow, with the freedom of the city, in recognition especially of his impor- tant services as Under-Secretary for the Colonies, Minister of Education, and Chief Secretary for Ireland. The Lord , Provost made the presentation. Mr. Forster in replying, said, to any man who cared about education, it was a plea- sure to find among the citizens of Glasgow the dermination 1 to have education. He was astonished to find such a great - number of men from the working classes study in the U•ni- ' yersity. It was also gratifying that the people of Scotland -. held to their old conviction thateeecular instruction should not be separated from religious training. AN INTERESTING GATHERING : A THIEVES' SUPPER IoiATTENDED BY JUDGES.—Mr. Howard Vincent, Director of _ the Criminal Investigation Department, Scotland-yard, pre- sided on Tuesday night at a free supper given to 250 k.,.._ • liberated convicted thieves. The supper was spread in the R!!* new Mission Chapel in Great Wyld-street, one of the worst portions of the Drury-lane locality, and among the visitors _ were the Hon. Justice and Lady Denman, Mr. Justice Wat- kenenee kin Williams, the Earl of Fife, and several magistrates and • governors of gaols. The object of the gathering was to endeavour to reform and provide employment for liberated criminals. Mr. Howard Vincent, during the evening, dis- tributed prises, including twenty watches, to reformed PI criminals for whom employment had been found, and who bad retained thsir situations twelve months. THE " FREETHINKER " LIBEL Cese.—ln the Queen's Bench Division of the High Court of Justice, Mr. Justice Hawkins, Mr. Justice Stephen, and Mr. Justice Wathin Williams, sitting at Westminster, had before them on Mon- day an application in the case of "The Queen v. Bradlaugh and others '—the case of the prosecution of Mr. Charles Bradlaugh, M.P. for Northampton, and other defendants, for blasphemous libels published in the paper called the ,IPP Freethinker.—Mr. Avory, renewing the application he made on Saturday, when it was held to be out of order in connec- tion with the demurrer of Mr. Bradlaugh, now asked their Lordships, on behalf of Mr. Ramsay, one of the defendants, I for leave to demur and plead over in resdect of certain ' counts in the the indictment to which Mr. Ramsay took ex- ception.—Their Lordships, however, considered that the ' objections were of too technical a character, and the appli- e cation was refused. THE COVENTRY VICAR'S RATE.—IrI response to a circular letter by the Mayor of Coventry, £3,200 bas been paid into Lloyd's Bank by the voluntary subscribers to the fund I: ' raised by his worship for the abolition of the vicar's rate for the parish of Holy Trinity, Coventry. The vestry of the parish have adopted a petition in favour of the bill for the repeal of the Act 19 George 111., c. 57, under which the rate has been collected. It was at the same meeting for- mally made known that the Ecclesiastical Commissioners had P ag £lOO perperpetuity upon the e vicar of the parish and his successors. The Bishop of Worcester has rendered material aid in the obtaining of this grant. The bill, of which notice has been given, provides for the repeal of the existing Act, for the maintenance of iI i the vicar on the payment to the feoffees of the Church Estate or trustees to be appointed of £4,200, and fixes the 1- stipend of the vicar at• £5OO per annum, and makes the payment of this salary a first charge on the Church Estate. SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A MEMBER OP PARLIAMENT. At Ramsgate Police Court, on Tuesday, Mr. Geo. Hemp- . den Whalley, M.P. for Peterborough, appeared to answer a charge of having obtained two sums of £l2 10s. and £5 re- epectively from Mrs. Colley, Albion Hotel, Ramsgate, by. . false pretences. Mrs. Colley deposed to defendant staying at the hotel in August and September last and obtaining - several sums of money, among them being the amounts mentioned in the charge in exchange for cheques, which were returned dishonoured. After some further evidence, Mr. Learoyd addressed the bench on behalf of defendant, Who, he stated, was in an unfortunate position, and had been . deprived of his income and fortune by a suit in Chancery, 1r.07" and had been compelled to file a petition for liquidation. Mr. Link was called, and stated that he had acted as Mr. Whalley's financial agent. During the pest year his firm had consented to cheques being drawn on them by defen- dant, and in every instance where he thought it ;vas justifi- able they were paid. He had refused to honour Mrs. Colley's cheque because he thought it was excessive, and beeause he received no advice.—The charEs was dismissed,

- FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE. A Lyons telegram says :—Prince Krapotkine was arrested on Thursday morning, at Thonon, and has been lodged in gaol. No fewer than fifteen of the women who were injured by the explosion of cartridges in Ment Yalerien (Paris) have

itself for clearing the ground of facts from the error with which a shameless misrepresentation of history had clouded the usually clear right of Russian public opinion." i A Berlin telegram of Thursday's date says :—"The North German Gazette' to-day refers to the observation made in an article of the Gobs on the 7th inst. to the effect that Prussia ; was the first to commence works of fortification and arma- ments on the eastern frontier, and that Russia was thereby compelled to take correspondine. measures. The semi-official I organ says any Government has indubitably the right to arrange its defensive measures as it may think fit, and no ; one, not even the Cologne Gazette, could regard this as affording ground for complaint, or as signifying preparation for immediately impending wars. It is true, however, that I frontier fortifications though defensive are at the same I time useless for attack. They serve to some extent the same purpose as the arming of war vessels. In view of increased penetrating power of artillery, armour plates are • being made stronger, and the increasing offensive strength of the empire makes the necessity of stronger defensive positions felt on the other side of the frontier. This, how- ever, just as little constitutes a symptom of the insecurity of peace as would the strgngthening of armour plates on the war vessels by England and France afford ground for appre- hension in regard to the relations between those two coun- tries. The National Gazette states that the contemplated movements of troops on the Prusso-Russian frontier will be made with the object of stationing larger garrisons of in- fantry, and eventually also of artillery, on the frontier ter- ritory. The Gazette adds that the erection of large barracks is projected, and that it is also intended to lay second lines of rails on several of the eastern railways."

The Berlin correspondent of the Times declared that, not- withstanding the visit of M. de Giers to Berlin, the relations between Germany and Russia are of a very mysterious and

unsatisfactory character. M. Bontoux, the founder of the Union Gen&ale—the great financial institution which failed some months ago— has been sentenced to five years' imprisonment on various charges of fraud. His college M. Feder receives a sisnilar

sentence. According to a Vienna correspondent, no proposals have yet been snbmitted by England to the Powers with regard to the international control of the Suez Canal, but an impression prevails that such proposals may be

made soon. Those Powers which have denounced their existing treaties with Turkey are invited by the Porte in a semi- official manner, to agree to certain modifications by which it is believed by the authorities at Constantinople that commerce will be facilitated and the revenue of the Otto-

man Empire increased. The Calcutta correspondent of the Times states that the Indian Education Commission have reassembled in Cal- cutta, and are now devising a scheme for the distribution of the final work among committees. Six committees will be formed ; and when the mass of evidence collected has been digested, recommendations of the suggested legislation will

be-rnade. A correspondent of the Times, telegraphing from Durban, gives currency to a report from Madagascar, dated the 9th inst., to the effect that a murderous attack was made by some natives about three months since, near Tullear, on two Englishmen. One of the two was killed. The survivor escaped, and is now there. The object of the assassins in this particular case was plunder, but the general temper of the natives towards Europeans is hostile. Anaav CHANGES IN Faarrez.—A decree just issued by the French Minister of War, affords a fresh illustration of the minor inconveniences to which the frequent changes of government in France give rise. The white gloves of the troopers, the abolition of which was ordered by General Farre, the late minister, are to be reinstated in favour. It appears that the order for their suppression had not even had time to be carried into effect. DARING RAILWAY OUTRAGE IN ITALY.—On the arrival of the train from Rome at six p.m. on Saturday, at Cassl- nuvo, the ticket station before Naples, two gentlemanly- dressed persons entered a first-class smoking carriage in which a lawyer and a goods inspector were travelling.. As soon as the train went at full speed the strangers, with dag- gers drawn, robbed them of their watches, money, and valuables, inflicting some slight wounds in the struggle. When the train slackened speed near Naples, the robbers jumped from the carriage and escaped across the fields. A telegram from Sydney, New South Wales, announces that the general election has resulted in the return of a large majority against the Government. Of the 108 mem- bers of whom the Legislative Assembly is composed, 80 members of the new Chamber belong to the Opposition, and 20 are supporters of the present Government. The Hon. James Watson, Colonial Treasurer and Minister for Finance and Trade; the Hon. Dr. Renwick, head of the Department of Mines; and the Hon. W. J. Foster, Minister of Justice, have failed to obtain seats in the new Parlia- ment. The jubilee of 300 years of Russian rule over Siberia was celebrated in St. Petersburg on Monday. The exact date of the annexation of the region subjugated by Yermak and his Cossacks is, observes a St. Petersburg correspondent, altogether unknown to Russian history. All that is known is that between the 28th of October and the 27th December, 1582, the Moscovite Czar Ivan the Terrible received a mes- senger from Yermak, and accepted dominion over the country, which had been voluntarily subdued by the Cos- sacks, under their celebrated chief. In this difficulty, it was thought fit to appoint the 18th of December, it being also the name-day of the young Heir-Apparent, Nicholas Alexandrovvitch, as a day ot thanksgiving and festivity throughout Siberia. ALSACE-LonnAINE.—A correspondent who is visiting Alsace-Lorraine sends some interesting information as to the state of public feeling, and the preparations which the new and the former owners have been and are making for the "war of revenge." The great fortress of Metz, the scene" of Bazaine's tame surrender, has been made practi- cally Impregnable and Strasburg, as is well known, is in a condition to bid defiance to any attack. The French, on their side, are working with unremitting energy to place a barrier across the path of an invading army. The people of Metz do not appear to be hopeful of the chances of the struggle which is regarded as inevitable. They made not the slightest protest when the official order was given that the divines in the various churches should preach in the German tongue. The correspondent remarks that the deter- mination of Germany to retain its hold on the conquered provinces is materially aided by the conviction existing in the minds of the peasantry, the only element almost now remaining, that nothing is to be hoped for from Republican France. What sentiment of a political character they possessed was Imperialist, and with the disappearence of the Empire their sympathy towards the Government at Paris languished towards extinction. THE STATE OF EGYPT. A considerable number of " political " prisoners who were in custody at Damietta have been pardoned by the Khedive. Arabi and lais fellow exiles will start for Ceylon on Monday next. . The paper El Ahram announces that Arabi will receive an allowance of not less than £3OO and not more than £5OO per annum. His wife will join him in Ceylon after her con- finement. About 80 persons in all will accompany the rebel leader to Ceylon. Lord Dufferin has laid before the Egyptian Government a scheme of reform for the native courts of justice. He pro- poses that the tribunals shall be presided over by European judges, and that the code shall be as far as possible similar to that administered by the International tribunals. AN INDIAN MASSACRE. SEVEN FY-FIVE PERSONS KILLED. It seems from accounts just received from North Mexico, dated the 7th instant, that a shocking massacre has been perpetrated by the Apache Indians, the victims numbering some 75 souls, while, in addition to these, a number of women and girls were carried off. The place attacked was Cacas Grande, on which a horde of about 500 Indians swept down, having come direct across the border. The little town was completely taken by surprise, and the inhabitants could offer but feeble resistance. About 75 persons were killed, after which the Indians set about plundering the valuables of the victims, also breaking into their dwellings. The bodies of the unfortunate Mexicans were quickly divested of their clothing and any articles of jewellery. The murdered people were amongst the meet prominent and wealthier families of the town. As soon as possible word of the terrible outrage was conveyed to the authorities, and a number of troops were despatched to the scene. The Indians had carried off several girls and wotr en, and some time before the troops arrived had left with their plunder. Having such a long start of the troops, it was not expected hat the latter would be able to capture them.

div.head: WAR ALARMS ON THE CONTINENT,
div.p: WAR ALARMS ON THE CONTINENT,

Great attention has been bestowed during the last few days upon statements which have been published in London and Cologne with regard to the possibility of a war between Austria and Russia, in which Germany would cer- tainly be involved. The official Abendpost of Vienna says that these statements bear " the stamp of improbability," and it protests that they have excited an amount of interest which they do not deserve. The Gotos a few days ago twitted Germany with having " deserted " Russia at the Berlin Congress. The North German Gazette replies that such attacks are unjust, because Germany supported all the Russian demands which were "officially" put forward, and might have gone further if Russia had thought fit to call upon her. A Reuter's telegram front Berlin says that the determina- tion of the German Government to maintain the alliance with Austria receives unmixed approval from the entire German press. The Catholic organ Germania says on the subject that the prolongation of the treaty will act as an effectual bar to Planslavist intrigues, te Russian extension aspirations, and to French plans of revenge. From Pesth it is reported by telegraph that in the Lower House of the Hungarian Diet on Wednesday, a member of the extreme Left questioned the Government regarding the condition ef foreign affairs. M. Tisza, the Premier, replied that newspaper reports on the subject were partly exaggera- ted and partly incorrect, and he declared that the peace of Europe was in no way threatened. The Minister added that he was not at the present moment aware of anything which tended to diminish the hopes hitherto entertained of the maintenance of peace. A Berlin telegram says :—The North German Gazette, referring to an article recently published in the Moscow Gazette on the relation between Germany and Russia, states 1 that the utterances of the journal in question have been hailed in political circles in Berlin with the greater satis- faction since they may be assumed to represent the views of leading personages in St. Petersburg. It then proceeds: —"The former misunderstandings mentioned by the Moscow Gazette were artificially produced and fostered by unquiet politicians and newspapm, the responsible directors of affairs in the two Empires being ignorant of any such mis- understanding. Certain Russian publicists, however, suc- ceeded with the help of some persons holding an official position in clouding the judgment of their readers, and rendering them more susceptible to an arti- ficially created excitement. It is satisfactory that so important an organ as the Moscow Gazette under- takes to enlighten public opinion in Russia on the misunder- standings of the period. The historical logic of its state- ments and the practical views expressed will bear good ' fruit. The journey of M. de Giers was hailed with satis- faction in Germany. The cordiality with which he was received at Court and in the country accorded not only with the close personal relations of the statesmen of the two Empires, but it was also the natural expression of the rela- tion subsisting between the two Cabinets. The hope ex- pressed by the Moscow Gazette that the meeting between H. de Giers and Prince Bismarck would clear the way for a mutual understanding was in nowise necessary as regards the two Ministers. div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

- --- At several collieries in Warwickshire, coal has been advanced in price to the extent of sd. per ton. There is in some parts of the district a brisk demand for coal, no doubt cansed by the severe weather which has been experienced during the present week. THE RECENT FAILURES IN THE TINPLATE TRADE.—The recent heavy losses in the tinplate trade and the suspension of several important South Wales firms have resulted in the stoppage of 28 works. The total liabilities are £1,000,000 sterling, and the decrease in the production is estimated at 130,000 boxes per week. It is feared that great privation', will ensue amongst the workmen. Serious disturbances have occurred in connection with the strike at the Bestwood Colliery, near Nottingham, and at the Town Hall, OR Wednesday, 18 persons were fined 10s. each for rioting and interfering with the police, who have been protecting the men who refused to come out on strike. MINERS AND THE OUTPUT. A national conferene miners was opened at Leeds on Tuesday afternoon, for the consideration of the question of the restriction of the out put. Delegates were present from Yorkshire Staffordshire Durham, Lancashire, Northumberland, Derbyshire, North Wales, 'Forest of Dean, Fife, and Clackmannan, represent- ing 257,000 men. Mr. Benjamin Pickard, of Barnsley, was elected president, and Mr. Thomas Ashton secretary. After the adoption of standing orders for the guidance of the meeting, the conference adjourned. At the sitting on Wed- nesday it was unanimously resolved that no collier or other workman engaged underground in coal getting, except those who are riecessarily engaged for the safety of the mines, should work more than five days or shifts in each week. It was also resolved that in double pits, where there is but one shift for boys, the hours of coal getters, Sec., remain as at present; but where there are two shifts of boys for two of coal getters, the hours of the latter be not more .than eight from bank to bank.—At the conference on Thursday, reso- lutions were passed affirming the intention of the miners not to discuss an immediate advance in wages either of 10 or 15 per cent., and leaving it to each district to carry on the regulation of output in the manner they consider de- sirable; also that the best time to carryout the resolution on the question of restriction was from February let, or, where sliding scales are in operation, at the earliest, oppor- tunity consistent with the arrangements. A resolution was afterwards adopted empowering the secretary to summon a meeting at Manchester if found neceseary. THE Lanourt MARKET.—In the labour market this week there is no appreciable change, and in nearly all the indus- trial centres the workpeople are fairly employed. In Lon- don the building trade this week has been fairly brisk, and -extensive preparations are being made for the new year. At Birmingham the hardware trade is brisk, and overtime is Ithe rule. For bridge and roofing materials and electric light fittings there is a brisk demand. The Wolverhampton finished iron manufacturers are fairly busy, the pig iron trade is brisk, and the coal trade is fairly active. At New- castle-on-Tyne the iron trade is steady, and shipping also. At Barnsley the mills and foundries are kept well going, and the coal trade is steady. In Cornwall mining is depressed. At Darlicgton the plateniakers have decided to lay off their works for a week to reduce the production. The coal trade is steady. At Barrow-in-Furness the hematite pig iron trade is quiet. At the Hartlepools iron, shipbuilding, and marine engineering works are on full time, other trades are in a fairly healthy condition. The textile trades show no material change. At Bradford spinners are only on regular time, although in Botany yarns there is an active business. At Kidderminster the looms are busy, and the weavers are trying to exclude strangers. At Leeds trade generally is fairly good, and increased business is anticipated at the new year. The Nottingham lace trade is fairly active, and a good spring trade is anticipated. At Leicester the silk elastic web trade is good, and also the hosiery trade, but the shoe trade is flat. At Northampton. Stafford, and Nor- wich the shoe trade is very quiet. At Halifax there is no change, spinners being only engaged on sorting orders, and at Manchester trade is steady.—Labour Netes. THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADES.—Although there was a good attendance on 'Change on Tuesday buyers showed but little disposition either to give ont orders or to make offers. Consumers who have iron to go on with are disinclined to place out further orders at present, not only in view of the approaching holidays, but also because they believe they have more to gain by waiting, and until the turn of the year it is not likely there will be any material change in the condition of the market. Lancashire makers of pig iron who have not yet issued any revised lists are practically doing nothing, as their old rates of 495. to 505., less 2, delivered equal to Manchester are altogether out of the market, and offers are not made to test what they would take. In distant brands a few odd sales of foundry iron are made on the basis of 485., less 21, delivered here, but forge qualities are not inquired for, and it is doubtful whether more than 475. could he realised. Finished-iron makers report exceedingly few new orders coming in, and old contracts are rapidly being run off; there is, however, no material yielding in prices, bars de- livered here remaining at about SO 103. per ton.— The increased activity which was imparted to the coal market by the recent severe weather, is still being main- tained. House fire coals are in tolerably good demand; other classes of fuel for iron-making and steam purposes are also moving off moderately well, and pits are better em- ployed than of late. Supplies, however, are still in excess of requirements, and in many cases colliery proprietors find it very difficult to maintain their full rates. The average prices at the pit mouth are about as under : Best coal, lOs to 103 6d ; seconds, 7s 9d to 8s &l; common house tire coals, Gs 6d to 7s; steam and forge coals 6s to 6s 6d ; good burgy, 4s 9d to 5s 3d; and good qualities of slack from 3s Od up to 4s 3d per tan. The more favourable weather for shipping has given a little stimulus to this branch of trade, but there is still no great amount of business doing, and prices both at Liverpool and Garston remain compara- tively low.

div.head: NATIONAL LIB EiAL FEDERATION.
div.p: NATIONAL LIB EiAL FEDERATION.

• -- The annual meetings of the National Liberal Federation were held on Tuesday at Ashton-under-Lyne. At the after- noon meeting, when delegates in large numbers from all parts of the country were in attendance, Mr. H. F. Pease presided. Amongst those present were Mr. W. Summers, M.P., Mr. W. Woodall, M.P., Mr. H. Lee, M.P., and Mr. Joseph Arch. Resolutions were passed congratulating Mr. Gladstone on the completion of his fiftieth year of parlia- mentary life, advocating the extension of the franchise to the counties, expressing the necessity for land reform and for the introduction of a bill dealing with corrupt parctices at elections. The report presented detailed the work of the Federation during the year, and expressed a hope that now that the rules of procedure had been amended attention might be given to the work of domestic legislation, which had been so long delayed. A great meeting was held in the evening, at which Mr. A. E. Reyner presided. There were also present the Right Hon. J. Chamberlain, Mr. Jesse Collings, M.P., Professor Stuart, of Cambridge, and Mr. Joseph Arch, all of whom addressed the meeting, as well as other gentlemen.—Mr. Chamberlain said that such an organisation as theirs was a very powerful instrument in the hands of the party of progress, and was part of that great democratic movement which bad broadened the foundatkns of liberty and done so much to establish the rights of the people. He defended the Egyptian campaign on the ground that it was necessary to uphold our highroad to India, but said that the Government had no intention of maintaining a 'permanent protectorate in Egypt. When we had secured peace, security, and good order; the reform of the tribunals, and reasonable security for the liberties of the Egyptian people, then our soldiers might retire, leaving behind them institutions capable of expansion and development. The day had passed when Lord Beaconsfield had stated that the policy of the British Government em- braced the extension of the empire, for our empire was already big enough. and our possessions 'sufficiently ample. He regretted the tone recently taken by the French Govern- ment and press, but thought that there was nothing in our policy, when clearly understood, which differed from the policy of enlightened Frenchmen, namely, the preservation of order and independence. With regard to Ireland, past experience had taught two lessons—one to Irish agitators, that no party in England sympathised with or tolerated out- rage and crime; and the other to English statesmen, that we should not turn a deaf ear to Irish wrongs and Irish grievances until we were forced to listen to them by the pressure of. calamity or lawless agitation. Athough things were improving in Ireland, our work would not be finished so long as Irishmen in their country were deprived of rights and privileges conceded to Englishmen and Scotchmen, but he hoped that by patience and justice we might ultimately succeed in making the whole population of the three king- doms a united and happy people. The new rules of proce- dure would give Parliament a chance of doing its work pro- perly, and if they found that obstruction was not abeo- Intely stopped, one thing was certain, that sooner or later the people would insist that effective means should be taken to restore its efficiency to Parliament, and to make it the true exponent of the will and wishes of the country.
