div.head: DISTRICT NEWS.
div.p: DISTRICT NEWS.

CROFT. PRIZE DISTRIBUTION A.T CROFT BOARD SCHOOL.—The annual entertainment and prize distribution took place at the above school on Friday evening week, under the patronage and presence of the members of the School Board. The school-room had been beautifully and tastefully decorated for the occasion by the headmaster, pupil teachers, scholars, and a few friends; and a platform had been erected to seat upwards of 80 children. Close to the platform stood a table on which were the prizes, consisting of handsome books. There was a good audience, and the Rev. T. H. Kirkham, M.A., F.R.S., the chairman of the School Board, having taken the chair, songs and recitations were given by the children in a highly creditable manner, under the conduc- torship of the headmaster, Mr. R. A. Davies, who also accompanied some of the songs on the pianoforte. The chairman then distributed the prizes, and the proceedings were brought to a close about half-past ten o'clock with the singing of the National Anthem.

FRODSHAM. FRODSHAISI LITERARY AND DEBATING SOCIETY.—A meet- ing of this society was held in the girls' school, Church- street, Frodsharn, on Monday evening, when the chair was taken by Charles Reynolds, Esq., J.P., and the Rev. J. M. Bamford read an excellent paper, the subject being "Which is the best policy as a rule of life, to cultivate a suspicious mind or to cherish confidence in honour?" .
HUYTON.

UPSETTING A HIIITTON DOCTOR. John McDermot, a carter for the Albion Brewery, Prescot, was charged at Prescot Petty Sessions, on,Tuesday, with being drunk while in charge of a horse and cart.—Mr. J. 0. Swift defended.— Dr. Pacher, of Huyton, stated that about half-past six in the evening, of the Bth inst., he was driving along Derby- road, Prescot, on his way home from a visit to Dr. Hall, when defendant, who was coming from the direction of Liverpool with a horse and lurry, pulled the rope or rein of his horse and drew his cart in front of the conveyance. The consequence was that the two vehicles became locked, and he (Dr. Pacher) was thrown over the splashboard and be- tween the hind legs of his horse. He was bruised black and blue by the fall, and it was a wonder he was not killed. His coachman was also thrown out. Defendant went off without offering any assistance. Shortly afterwards he went to the brewery stables and saw defendant, who was so far gone in drink that he could not articulate properly or stand erect. Mr. Green, assistant for Dr. Hull, who accompanied Dr. Thacker to see defendant, stated that defendalt was drunk.—Defendant denied being drunk, and called a num- ber of witnesses to show that he was perfectly sober, and tbat the collision with Dr. Pacher's conveyance wag an accident, the night being dark.—Defendant was fined 103. and 17s. ed. costs.

HALTON. ROBBERY BY i BEERHOCSB KEEPER.—Joseph Taylor, beerhouse keeper at Halton, was charged at the Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, with stealing, on the 28th ult., four game fowls, value 9s, one hamper, and a bag, the pro- perty of John Weir, farmer; and, further, with stealing four Hamburg hens, one hamper, and one bag, the property of Henry Whelow, on the same day.—The two prosecutors attended a sale of poultry at Mr. Darbyshire's farm, and bought the fowls mentioned, which they placed for a time in a convenient place near the building where the sale was going on. About six o'clock in the evening the poisoner went to John Peter Glover, and wanted him to carry the fowls produced down to where his trap was. He assisted, and he ultimately saw the prisoner put the fowls into the trap and drive away with a Mr. Leather, and a man named Haddock. On being charged with the robbery, prisoner said "I did not steal them; some one put them in my trap." —Mr. Moore, who appeared for the prisoner, produced testimonials of the prisoner's previous good character, and asked their worships to take a lenient view of the case, as he had evidence to show that the prisoner was drunk when the robbery was committed.—The Bench said the evidence was conclusive, but they would dismiss the case on the payment of damages not exceeding 405., and such costs as the court might think reasonable. • LYMM.

LYMII LIBERAL Assoct—moN.—We append copy of a letter received from Mr. Gladstone's private secretary in response to the resolution adopted at the meeting at Lymm on the 12th inst :—" 10, Downing-street, Whitehall, Dec. 16, 1882.—Sir,—I am directed by Mr. Gladstone to request you to convey his best thanks to the members of the Lymm Liberal Association for their kind congratulations.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, G. LEVESON GOWER.—J. A. Swanwick, Esq." IMPUDENT ROBBERY AT HEATLEY.—A youth named Philip Hughes was charged at Altrincham Petty Sessions, on Monday, with stealing a fowl, property of J. Simpson, at Heatley,.Lymm, on the 13th December. Prisoner had been employed at the thrashing machine, and about half-past seven on Friday night he asked prosecutor's son if the dog was about, and wanted a strap for the machine. He went for the strap and came back. He looked into the place where tire son was, and soon after he heard a flutter. He saw prisoner putting something under the turnip cutter, and on getting a light found the fowl produced. Prisoner was fined 103 and costs 31s, or 14 days' imprisonment in default of payment.

div.head: NORTHWICH. The Northwich Rural Sanitary Authority is considering a suggestion to supply Anderton with water from a spring on the estate of Lord Stanley.
div.p: NORTHWICH. The Northwich Rural Sanitary Authority is considering a suggestion to supply Anderton with water from a spring on the estate of Lord Stanley.

NANTWICH. An inquiry has been held at Nantwich in regard to the death of an infant, named Elizabeth Ellen Sutton. The child was two months old, and appeared very healthy, but on Friday died suddenly. The Coroner (Mr. Chnrton) ex- pressed an opinion that the child succumted to heart disease, to which young children are subject.—The jury rbturned a Yerdict of natural death.

OVER. A CHESHIRE CENTENARIAN.—There died last week at Beauty Bank, near Over, an old woman, named Betty Booth, who had reached the age of 103 years. She enjoyed very good health up to within a few weeks of her death. In the corn harvest of this year she reaped four sheaves of corn—two on a Saturday and two on the Monday following; and in her 101st year she attended a tea meeting in her own neighbourhood, and sang by herself one of Watt's hymns she had learnt when a girl at school. It is a somewhat singular circumstance that two neighbours of hers, aged 75 and 89, died the same week, and that all three had been servants and were tenants of Lord Delamere, of Vale Royal. The Congregational Church, Over, having long been in want of a good instrument, has at last got an organ of which neither organist or choir need be ashamed. On the occasion of its opening on Wednesday evening, by J. F. Swift, Esq., of Liverpool, there was an organ recital and concert by the members of the choir and some professionals whom the conductor, J. D. Harris, Eq., of Nantwich, secured. The organ has been erected and built by Messrs. John Stringer and Co, Hanley, and contains the following stops :—Great Organ: Oven diapason, gunba, stop diapa- I son, clarabella, principal, flute, twelfth and fifteenth. Surd/ Organ: Open diapason, lieblich, gemshorn, kerauldpben, voix celecte and oboe. Pedal Organ: Grand;bourdon, and there are three couplers to unite the whole swell to great, and the swell to pedal. The organ is a credit to its builders, and the town of Winsford. Only one drawback exists ; there remains a debt on the instrument, but no doubt it will be wiped off ere long.

RAINFORD. • ATTACH ON A CONSTABLE AT RAINFonD.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Tuesday, a man named Wm. Fair- hurst, was charged with having assaulted P.C. Ratcliffe, at Rainford, on the 6th August, last year. It appeared that on the occation referred to the officer had interfered in a quarrel, in which the prisoner was concerned, at the Red Cat beerhouse. The prisoner had refused to desist, and the officer was attempting to take him into custody. He behaved very violently, and on getting out into the road was assisted by a crowd of people. Stones were thrown, one of which struck the prisoner and knocked him senseless. The people then attacked the officer, deprived him of his handcuffs, and carried away the prisoner, who had been no more seen till he was apprehended on Monday at Ashton. Prisoner was remanded till Friday, bail being allowed. STEALING AN OIL CAN AT RIINFORD.—At the St. Helens County Petty Sessions, on Monday, a young man, named John Kirman, was charged with having stolen an oil can, valued at 2s, the property of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Company.—lt appeared that about four o'clock on the morning of the 16th inst. a police officer bad noticed the prisoner on a road near Rainford Junction railway station, and, being suspicious of his appearance, took him beside a lamp and searched him, and found the oil can in question concealed about his person in pieces. He took him into custody, and afterwards found that the can had been stolen from the railway station.—Prisoner said he could not give any account as to how the stoles property had come to be in his possession, and was consequently fined 20s and costs or in default 14 days' imprisonment. ALLEGED POACHING NEAR RAINFORD.-011 Monday, at the St. Helens County Petty Sessions, before Mr. Penning- ton, Major Pilkington, and Mr. J. C. Gamble, two men, named Thomas Darbishire and Thomas Rosbottom, were charged with poaching near Rainford on the 30th ult.—Mr. Marsh prosecuted on behalf of Lord Derby, and Mr. Swift defended.—A witness named James Agnewo farmer, said he had been standing on the day in question en his own land and saw the two defendants going across a field which was rented by his father from Lord Derby, and go out on to the lane. Is soon as they got/there he saw a hare in the pos- session of one of tbem.—Another witness named James Johnson spoke to having seen both the defendants in the lane mentioned on the day in question.—Mr. Swift con- tended that no evidence had been brought forward on which the Bench could convict.—After some deliberation the Bench recalled the witness Agnew, against which Mr. Swift protested, as the case ought, he said, to be dealt with upon the evidence brought forward by Mr. Marsh. If the Bench had any doubt they should give the defendants the benefit of the doubt.—Major Pilkington said they knew sufficient law to know that if they had any doubt they had a perfect right to recall any witness to try and clear that doubt up • if they could not clear it up they would give the defendants the benefit of the doubt.—Mr. Peanington and Mr. Gamble concurred in this opinion, and Agnew was questioned as to his being sure it was a hare which the defendants had in their possession.—Ultimately the case was dismissed.

STRETTON. PEnmirrnm DRIJNICENNESS.-0/1 Tue.sday, it the Pa bury Petty Sessions, Thomas Hindley was charged with permitting drunkenness on his licensed premises at Stretton on the 30th October. SuPerintendent iVilliatnson stated that a man named Mitchell had been convicted of being

div.head: WINWICK.
div.p: WINWICK.

TRESPASSING IN PERSEIT OF GAME: AN OLD SCORE.... At Warrington Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, James Hill, of Winwick, was charged on a warrant with trespassing in pursuit of game on the 2nd December of last year. P.C. Rigby said that on the 2nd December last year he found the prisoner and another man, who had been before the magistrates and fined, on the land of Mr. John Pollitt, in pursuit of game. They had seven nets and two ferrets. Prisoner did not answer to his summons, and had been absent from the locality ever since the offence was com- mitted, and it was only a few days since that they had been able to capture him. Prisoner was fined 18s and costs, in all 263.

ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS. NEW MAGISTRATES FOR CREwE.—The Lord Chancellor has added the names of Mr. Charles Dick, manager of the London and North-Western Railway Works at Crewe • Mr. George Whale, assistant locomotive superintendent o the London and North-Western Railway; and Mr. Richard Pedley, merchant, to the commission of the peace for the borough of Crewe. There was an interesting discussion on "ensilage " en 'Saturday at the annual meeting of the Chester Farmers' Club. One of the speakers, Mr. T. Parker, made the satis- factory statements that the Cheshire farmers were now able to show a clean bill of health in respect to their flocks and herds, and in the prospect of a long winter they had their buildings and stackyards fuller of store than had been the case for a long time past. STARVATION IN CHESTER.—The very severe weather which has prevailed for some time past has been the cause of a great deal of misery and destitution in Chester and the neighbourhood. A case ,heard at the Chester County Police Court, on Saturday, sadly illustrates some of the afflictions of the poor, and the temptations which beset them. John Kenny, a labourer, was charged with having stolen nibs. of coal, the property of the London and North Western Railway Company. The prisoner was caught in the act, and confessed his guilt. The theft, however, was not a vulgar one. The prisoner's wife and children had neither fire nor food at home, and, driven to desperation, he went out, like John Valjean, and risked his own liberty for the sake of his family. Police Sergeant Leah, who arrested the prisoner, on visiting his house, found that there was neither food, fire, nor furniture in the place. There were three sacks which were used for a bed, and the prisoner's three children were eating a turnip; the prisoner's wife had nothing. They were in a terrible state of want and misery. The Bench thought the case was an exceedingly sad one, but they felt bound to protect the property of the public, and as the prisoner had been previously convicted, he was sentenced to ten days' imprisonment.

THE COMPULSORY POWERS OF SCHOOL BOARDS. IMPORTANT DECISION. In the Queen's Bench Division of the High Court of Justice, on Tuesday, the Lord Chief Justice Mr. Justice Field, Mr. Justice Hawkins, Mr. Justice Stephen, and Mr. Justice Watkin Williams had before them the cases of " 'VVinyard v. Toogood " and "Hance v. Fortnum." These cases came up in the form of special cases stated for the opinion of the court by magistrates of London and Liver- pool, and raised an important question in regard to the powers of school boards under the Education Act of 1876. The question in both cases turned entirely on the construc- tion of the 11th section of the Act, which provides that in the case of a child alooye the age of five years and under the age of 14, who under the Act is prohibited from being taken into full-time employment, the parent who neglects to pro- vide such child with efficient elementary instruction may have an attendance order made upon hirrk. The magistrates, following a previous decision of the court in the case of "Saunders v. Crawford," held that the children of the parents against whom the School Boards proceeded in these two cases were not children who under the Act were prohibited from being taken into fall-time employment. They found that the fathers had neglected to provide efficient education for their children, and that they were liable if the children came within the operation of the 11th section, but, holding that the section did not apply, they decided that an attendance order could not be made against the parents. It was argued as against this decision that the words of the 11th section with regard to children prohibited from being taken into full-time employment applied equally to children prohibited from being taken into half-time employment or from being employed at all. The contention on the other side was that under the 11th section the child prohibited from being taken into full time employ- ment meant only the child who was permitted to be taken into half-time employment, and had no reference to the child prohibited from work altogether. Haying heard argu- ments on both sides, their Lordships unanimously reversed the decision of the courts below.

LOCAL BILLS IN PARLIAMENT. CI:MI:EIRE LINES COMMITTEIt.—This Bill is promoted to confer further powers upon the committee incorporated by the Cheshire Lines Act,lBts7, with regard especially to the holding and disposal Of lands in the townships of Walton and Toxtetla, and the parish of Liverpool, also in the parish of Frodsharn, Cheshire. Among the railway and other works authorized by the Act are a short branch in Warrington, the widening of the Stockport and Timperley branch, the widen- ing of the bridge of the Cheshire Midland branch at Knuts- fold, &c. Provision is made for changing the name of the committee to the Cheshire Lines Company, and it is pro- scribed that the works shall be completed within five years from the passing of the Act, subject to a penalty of xao a day beyond that period. The power of the cammittee for the compulsory purchase of lands is limited to three years. The Parliamentary agents for the Bill are Messrs. Wyatt, Hoskins, and Hooker. I LANCASHIRE PLATEWAY.—Amongst the private bills just deposited in the Parliamentary Bill Offices for next session is one promoted by Messrs. J. Bingham, T. Brocklebank, A. B. Forwood, J. Greenwood, A. Holt, T. D. Hornby, F. R. Leyland, and F. N. Reynolds for the incorporation of a company to construct and work platcways between Liver- pool and Manchester, with branches to Warrington, Old- ham, Ashton-under-Lvne, Rochdale, Walton-on-the-Hill;. Ashton-in-Makerfield, -Great Lever, Yarnworth, Chorley, Wigan, Penwortham, Blackburn, Burnley, and Old Accring- ton. Plateways are described as being railways, the plates or rails of which shall be so constructed as to admit the pas- sage thereon of rolling stock capible of travellint on ordin- ary country roads and the streets of towns, and also of ordinary railway rolling stock. The capital of the company is to be £0,000,000, in £2O shares, and the compulsory powers for the purchase of land are limited to five years. There is also a clause bolding the company not to dispossess labouring people of their houses without providing accom- modation for them elsewhere. Seven years is the period within which the works are to be completed. Passengers are not to be carried on these plateways, but only goods, and for the carriage of these, elaborate tables of toils are scheduled. Messrs. Thornley and Dismore, Liverpool, and Bircham and Co., London, are the solicitors for the bill ; Mr. J. C. Rees, Westminster, being the Parliamentary agent. WARRINGTON TRAMWAYS BlLL—This Bill, which has been deposited in the bill office of the House of Lords, pro- poses the construction of tramways in the borough of War- rington, and the neigLourhood thereof. It is proposed that the capital of the company shall be £50,000, in 5,000 shares of £lO each. The company is not to create debenture stock. The period for the completion of the work 13 proposed to be two years from the passing of the act. Messrs. Ridgway and Worsley, di 2, Cairo-street, Warrington, are solicitors for the bill, and Messrs. Darnford and Co., 38, Parliament- street, Westminster, the agents.

THE CIRCULATIOIsi OF NOTES UNDER £s.—Mr. William Fowler, M.P., addressed the members of the Institute of Bankers upon this question on Wednesday night, in the hall of the London Institution, Finsbury-circus. Sir John Lubbock, Bart., M.P., the president, occupied the chair.— Mr. Fowler said it was true, as to the greater operations of conareerc, the size of the bank notes now in use was of no consequence, because in their operations they did not prac- tically use bank notes at all. Bank business was done by instruments of credit, and not by means of cash or notes representing cash. He then proceeded to refer to one or two points in the history of this subject Lem 1793 up to the present time, remarking that throughout this long period £1 notes had been freely circulated in Scotland and Ireland, and were very popular in those countries. They clung to their small notes as an important part of their system. So, too, with regard to the Continent, the United States, India, and Australia. Mineowners, rail way directers and other employers of labour bad assured him that the carriage of large masses of gold coin for the payment of wages was a source of much inconvenience. It had been shown that every other sovereign was light, and that the probable cost of restoring English coin would fall not far short of £1,000,000; it was, then, obviously far more easy to maintain the value of the paper duly secured than of coin, which was being perpetually wore away. He Pro- posed that the issue department a the Bank of England. should issue a fixed amount of small notes against securities, and the Lalance sf such notes against bol on or coin [met to the issue department as at present. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, DECEMBER 23, 1882.

THE much-derided National Liberal Federation—ketter known, perhaps, as the "Birmingham Caucus " held its annual meeting at Ashton-under-Lyne this week. The organisation has now been in existence five years, having been founded in Birming- ham in the year 1877, when it received the countenance of Mr. GLADSTONE. Since its formation it has exercised a very potent in- fluence in stimulating Liberal thought and sentiment, and to it the Liberal party is in our opinion very much indebted. It may not in every detail meet with the approval of all Liberals, yet when we find a statesman such as Lord DERBY pronounce so decisively in its favour, as did his Lordship in Manchester last week, we may rest assured that in its essential particulars the organisation is a sound and safe one to accept generally as a guide. Our Conservative friends are never tired of condemning the Caucus, yet, strange to say, they are very fond of imitating it—in every borough and county they have intro- duced something analogous to it—but the success which has attended their efforts has been very limited, and to this fact may be traced much of the abuse heaped upon the Liberal Federation. As Mr. CHAMBERLAIN says, the Conservative copy of the Caucus is nearly perfect, yet there is something want- ing. "The body is there, but not a soul. The outline is there, but it is not filled up. The representatives are there, but they have no constituencies." The report presented to the Federation is scarcely so satisfactory as that of some previous years, for the reason that there has been very little legislation, still much useful work has been accomplished. The report refers with some degree of pride to the action taken by the Executive of the Federation with the view of defeating Mr. I MARRIOTT'S amendment to the Closure reso-

doubt not that before Christmas, 1884, arrives, Ireland will—mainly through the influence of the beneficent legislation of last session— be still more contented and peaceful. The season is one in which, even under the most depressing circumstances, everyone gives him- self or herself more or less tip to pleasure, but this is of course much more the case, when, as in the present instance, there is , nothing to disturb the even tenour of our ways. I An old writer very appropriately says this is the season when "quarrels are composed and 'fo,-gotten, old friendships are renewed and w,a;' necessary to rule Ireland with a ste-n hand, ,:nore especially after the Phoenix Park Support was consequently given to" trag-e dy, . -nt the Govetnm in passing the Protection of . .. Life and Prope7BilL some of the provisions :17 :tver, modified through the of which we,re , the Committee of the influence exercised - Federation. At the ie time the Federa s tion were not unmindfla .0f Ireland and the crying nee'emin.,-v for nz easures ' the wants of of relief. Hence we find th 5.4 Arrea.r: he' Act of the Government recited the ci;rdial syji- pathy of the organisation, and when the' fory majority of the House of Lords threate.ned the measure, the efforts of the Federation were put forth in its support. It very soon became evident—mainly in consequence the action of that body—that the country would not tolerate the House of Lords throw- ing out the measure, and we all know the result—the Tory majority, instead of throwing out the bill, deserted Lord SALISBURY and rescued themselves from the false and unten- able position into which the noble Marquis would have led them. Some people may b: inclined to doubt the loyalty of the Federa- tion, yet we find that when an attempt was made on the life of Her MAJESTY a resolution rejoicing at her providential escape—and in its term:; not less loyal than any resolution emanating from any gathering of Tories, who claim to have a monopoly of loyalty—imme- diately found its way to Royalty. Loyalty to the Crown and attachment to the Constitution are therefore qualities to be found in other than Conservative breasts. We learn also from the report of the Federation that two conferences have been held during the year, one at Newcastle-on-Tyne and the other at Nottingham. The object of these conferences is the diffusion of politi- cal information and the promotion of the work of Liberal organisation. That being so, it seems to us rather inconsistent that the meetings should have been held in towns noted for their Radical proclivities. We would suggest that these conferences should be held much oftener, and that they take place in constituences distinguished for their adherence to the principles of Conservatism. The adoption of such a course ought, we think, to tend to better results. The presence of the delegates in a Conservative constitu- ency would certainly lead to controversy ; controversy would be followed by the diffusion of. knowledge, which must ultimately lead to conversion. Amongst the political movements in which the Federation takes a special interest is that which has for its object the Reform of the Land Laws. To promote this object a special fund has been raised, and an appeal for aid issued to the public. The response, we are glad to know, has been generous, over L 5,000 having been subscribed; and when we find the persons interested in such a reform liberally subscribing of their substance towards its accomplishment, we may be satisfied they are in earnest, and that the time is not far distant when their liops will be realised. The dissemination of political literature and the providing of lec- turers on political subjects are healthy and invigorating features in the Federation, and these, we think, ought to be enceui aged more than they have hitherto been. The services of the lecturers are offered without charge to the associations desiring them, a fact which ought to be borne in mind by associations whose funds are not perhaps in the healthiest condition That is no bar, how- ever, to their receiving enlightenment on the leading political questiOns of the day from gentlemen well qualified to lead them. At the business meeting of the Federation held on Tuesday afternoon, resolutions were passed in favour of the extension of household suffrage in the counties, the development of local self-government, the suppression of corrupt practices at elections, reform of the land laws, the right of Mr. BRADLAUGH to take his seat for Northampton, and many other.kindred subjects. All these are ques- tions which must be settled in the near future, and now that the Rules of Procedure in the House have been reformed, we shall be very I much surprised if some of them are not I effectually dealt with next session._ Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, the President of the Board of Trade, presided at the evening meeting, and delivered a very stirring address. He made an able defence of the policy of the Govern- ment, of which he is a distinguished member; and he playfully dwelt on the desponding con- dition of the Tory party, who, he said, now rested their hopes on the success of the "False Prophet .in the Soudan" This is by no means an unhappy illustration. They have resorted to all sorts of shifts in order to raise their spirits. Mr. FORWOOD hoped to do a stroke of business for them at Liverpool by a new dodge, but Tory Liverpool could see through it and would have none of him. The Federation, as we Stated at the outset, is doing an excellent work, and it is entitled to receive, as it deserves, the support of all true Liberals. Meetings such as that of Tuesday have an influence far beyond the immediate circle to which the gathering is confined, and to us it seems a pity they are not held ' oftener. If the Federation had done nothing more than deliver constituencies from the domination of influential local coteries, or of Committees in London, in the selection of Parliamentary candidates, we contend that would be enough to warrant its existence. But it has done much more, and we feel sure that in years to come, when the franchise is extended, the organisation will be produc- tive of untold benefit to the Liberal cause. In itself it is thoroughly representative, and it possesses all the elements which conduce to success at elections.

CHRISTMAS, the greatest of the festivals throughout the ecclesiastical year, is now upon us, and it is a cause for rejoicing that the condition of things under which it will be celebrated is on the whole bright. For several years past it has been customary at each recurring Christmastide to deplore the state of trade, not unfrequently, too, has the political horizon given cause for alarm at this season, and at other times our foreign rela- tions have been a source of uneasiness. At present, however, we are at peace with all the world, there is a lull in political matters at home and consequently no fear of a crisis, ; and every branch of trade is fairly prosperous. Last Christmas the lawless state of _lreland was uppermost .in every person's mind, bsut now it is a pleasure to note the change in the condition of that unhappy country, and we

Ilutions ; -and the signal success which attended the efforts of the Federation in this direction we are all familiar with. The moving spirits of the organisation were not slow to detect the evils which would follow the adoption of the amendment of the mem- ber for Brighton, and their promptness in arousing Liberals to a sense of its dangers no doubt led to its defeat. It is a pleasure to note the action of the Federation with regard to Irish affairs. A body so Radical in its tendencies would scarcely be credited with giving any countenance to coercion, yet the Federation were not blind to the fact that it confirmed, and a universal spirit of charity and forgiveness is evoked." "Beggars," we are told, "have claims on our charity at this [ season, maugre all maxims of political economy, and must not be turned from our [ doors unrelieved" It is the season above all others for the exchano-e of mu:ual good _ wishes, which are all the more welcome and can be the better appreciated whcn there is [ peace on every hand, and joining in the general rejoicing, we cordially wish our readers collectively and individually, a very ." Merry Christmas."

The man of medicine seemed at last to triumph over the man of science, and the matter dropped on the understanding that the nuisance should be further inquired into.

Tuesday last was the anniversary of the adoption of the Free Libraries Act by the inhabitants of Runcorn, and a retrospective view of what has been achieved during the past .twelve months must, I think, be satisfactory to the most ardent advocate of the establishment of the library, and a crushing falsifica- tion of the statements of its opponents. Barely six months have elapsed since the library was opened. It now numbers over 700 members; the ordinary nioathly issue of books exceeds a thousand volumes, aud signs are not wanting that the "high water mark" has yet to be reaehed. One very gratifying feature is the willingness with which gentlemen add to the treasures that crowd the shelves of the library, which is already too large for its present cramped, situation. Ido not think I shall be overstating the figure if I say 150 volumes have been given during the past six months. The latest gift, however, exe ceeds them all. Mr. Hazlehuret's offer to establish a free reading. room in connection with the library, though it has taken many phaees since made, has recently assumed EC more tangible form, and there is every prospect that, ere long, the working population of Runcorn will be able to cultivate their taste for reading within the four walla of Waterloo House. Perhaps the greatest obstacle now to be overcome is the question of rent which was raised at the last meeting of the Library Committee, by Dr. Steele. Dr. Steele is of opinion that the Cemmissionern may with p/npriety ask the committee to pay a rent of £2O a year; 1)1;1 Mr. Handley, with a dafieitenaaa, which almost earrica cepa-L.4J on with it, states that the Commissioners cannot legally etea:.lnd It, and he. explieitly gives his reasons for his statt;: ments. It is, I have no doubt, Dr. Steele's desire to' act in order, and at the committee meeting on Tues- day he generously offered to pay £5 a year towards the rent, adding naively that Dr. MacDougall, whoee interest in the Library is well known, would have no objection to subscribing a similar sum, a suggestion which the worthy doctor did not seem to relish. How- ever the question of rent may be decided, Mr. Hazle- burst deserves tile gratitude of all true Rancornians for his munificent gift, whieh he has seemed to en- large in proportion as his first offer was adversely eriticised, and I am sure it is their earnest desire, as it is mine, that he may be soon again occupying a seat on the Board of Commissioners, and on the Free Libaary Committee. _ _ _ _

It is-gratifying to learn- that the efforts being me by the committee. of the- Runcorn Young Meth" Christian Association, to pre-ride a Christmas tea for the old people of the town, are so far crowned with success. The project meets on every hand with sym- pathy, which finds practical expression in gifts of money and "kind," and I hear that 600 aged folks, as a result, will be enabled to partake of a cheering meal.

Weeleyans will hail with pleasure the appointment of Mr. Thomas Norman to the office of steward of the Runcorn circuit (which was recently made), and under his stewardship I feel convinced the circuit finances will not suffer.

It is not often that a clergyman receives such a reprimand from his diocesan as that whic-h the Rev. C. E. Taunton, vicar of Ste John's, Harlow, has had administered to him by the Bishop of St. Albans; hope there are very few, if any, instances in which it is so well deserve]. The Rev. C. E. Taunton belongs to a breed of ecclesiastics who are rapidly becoming extinct, and the sooner the better. They are not troubled with any feelings of humanity themselves, and they presume that nobody else is. The Rev-. C. E. Taunton has distinguished himself by obstructing the funeral of a Nonconformist., and he did this by closing the churchyard gates, and compelling the procession to enter by another gate made for the purpose. The matter was brought under the notice of the Bishop by a Mr. Edwards, the Nonconformist minister who was conducting the funeral under the provisions of the Burials' Act, and his lordship promptly replied, ex- pressing disapproval of Mr. Taunton's proceedings, and begging the relatives of the deceased to accept his sympathy with them- under the painful circumstances which attended the burial. To the clergyman, the Bishop wrote :—" If the account is. true—and there seems no reason to doubt its substan- tial accuracy—you have attempted to evade the law in a manner hitherto unheard of, and, in my opinion, you have outraged all pious Christian feeling." The Home Secretary was also communicated with on the question, and his secretary writes expressing the con- fidence of Sir William Harcourt that "The severe and well-merited rebuke administered by the Bishop to the Rev. C. E. Taunton will have the effect of preventing, for the future, similar attempts to evade the law, which are equally an outrage on civil rights and Christian charity." I hope the censure will have this effect, but I am afraid that in the case of a person such as the Rev. C. E. Taunton it will not. I rather think the only means of awakening him to a know- ledge of his condition is to deprive him of his living, if that be possible, for he is utterly unworthy to hold it ; and I am sure that his offence is far more heinous then the wearing of any objectionable vestment or the genuflexions—which to some Churchmen are so irri- tating—of certain clergymen at the altar. THEFT FROM A. WIDNES GROCER'S S HOP.—A boy named James Murray was charged at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, with having on the 18th inst. stolen a bottle of sweets of the value of is. 7d., the property of George Wharton, grocer and provison dealer, Victoria-road, Widnes. —From something which was said to him, the prosecutor, who was having his tea, went into the shop; and discovered that a bottleof sweets had been taken from a shelf. He then went outside, atid seeing the prisoner running away, he followed and captured him. Before reaching the prisoner prosecutor had seen the former stoop down, and at that place he found the bottle of sweets produced.—The pri- soner denied having committed the robbery, stating that another boy was guilty of the offence.—The prosecutor expressed his belief that the bottle had been abstracted by other boys and handed to the prisoner.—The Bench sen- tenced the boy to six strokes with the birch rod. GOOD TEMPLARY AT Rusconx.—The Hope of Runcorn lodge of Good Templars have just celebrated the 13th anni- versary of the introduction of Good Templary into the town. It appears that the first lodge was held on the Ist December, 1869. A short time before this date some of the townsmen became interested in the Good Templary movement, which they saw carried on so successfully in neighbouring towns. They began to enquire, and the result was that a communi- cation was received from Mr. Joseph Matins, the Grand Worthy Chief Templar of England, who granted a charter on the temperance friends expressing their willingness to conduct a lodge. At a tea meeting held to celebrate the anniversary, about 50 members were present. The tea was provided by Sisters Mcßride and Wilsoy and Brother John Faulkner. After tea a degree temple was held, at which second and third degrees were conferred on several members. Then followed a miscellaneous entertainment, which opened with a short address by Brother Faulkner, W.C.T. Songs were given by Sister Hoskin and Brothers Coventry,Hughes, and Riley.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD: REDUCTION OF THE STAFF: On Thursday afternoon a special meeting of Widnes Local Board was held at the offices, Alford Chambers, for the pur-. pose of considering the "staff and market bye-laws." The Chairman (Mr. F. H. Gossage) presided, and there were also present*Messrs. Carey, Pankhurst, T. Handley, Dr. Booth, D. Wright, J. Midwood, Martley, Kershaw, Shuttleworth, Sadler, Webster, and Johnson. The members resolved themselves into a committee, and • the reporters were requested to retire. Wo have, however, been supplied with the following particulars. The first proposal was one to reduce the clerk's (Mr. Allen's) salary, and a long discussion ensued. Eventually it was decided that no alteration should be made, and his salary therefore still remains at £450. The emoluments of the clerks in the office also came under review, with the following result: The salary of Mr. Wilson was increased from £B5 to £95 ; of Mr. Reyes from £7O to £75; of Mr. Sankey from £39 to £52. It was decided to dispense with the services of Mr. Deanett, who has been empbyed in the office for a con- siderable number of years. No alteration was made in the other appointments of the Board. The advisability of appointing a law clerk was considered, but no action was taken. On the motion of Mr. Carey, seconded by Mr. D. Forster, the market bye-laws were adopted, an the Board rose.

"THE COMING END ": SERMON WIC THE REV. W. Ps-

TON, OF RUNCORN.—The first of course of Sunday night sermons, by the Rev. W. Preston, M.A., of Runcorn, was preached in Holy Trinity Church, on Sunday evening, on "The coming end." The discourse was founded on the text "Jerusalem shall be trodden down of the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles be fulfilled."

THE WO3IAN AND HER DoG AT WIDNES.—Mary L-edg- wick was summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednes- day, to answer a charge of keeping a dog without a license. The defendant lives in Gerrard-street, and a constable visit- ing the house discovered she was keeping a dog without license. In answer to his inquiries she said she had no money to purchase one and• that he would have a " good cheek " if he summoned her.—Defendant did not appear, and she was fined 53. and costs. RUNCORN LIBERAL ASSOCIATION AND MR. GLADSTONE'S JUBILEE.—Friday next is the anniversary of Mr. Glad- stone's entry in political life fifty years ago, and the " jubilee " is to be appropriately celebrated, by the Liberals of Runcorn. On the evening of that day a banquet will be held at Wilson's Hot and Mr. G. W. Latham of Bradwall Hall. Mr. E. G. Salisbury, of Chester, and other progniii.nt members of the party are expected to be present arid take part in the proceedingl., The number of ticket?, to bq izsued- will rlieessarily be jimited, ana. time kiesirous of paying , this tribute of respect to the brilliant career of the "grand old man" would do well to apply early to Mr. 0. Leak, the secretaiy to the association, who has charge of the arrange- ments.

WOMEN SETTLING THEIR DEBTS AT WIDNES.—II Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. Earle and Mr. Pilkington, Mrs. Murphy, who keeps a greengrocer's shop, was summoned by Mrs. Sarah Bennett, whose husband is a milk dealer in Widnes, for assaulting her on Saturday night, the 16th inst ; and Mrs. Murphy had issued a cross- summons against Mrs. Bennett, charging her with a simliar offence. Mrs. Bennett, on the night in question, went to Mrs. Murphy's house to ask for a sovereign which she alleged Mrs. Murphy had borrowed from her, when the defendant, without any provocation, struck her on the shoulder and knocked her on her back on the parapet. A number of witnesses were called, and gave evidence of a conflicting character, Mrs. Murphy alleging that Mrs. Beoett first struck her on the shin with her foot.—Case d:sllaissodi—Mr. Husband appeared for Mrs. Bennett. ROBBERV POTLTOB P 7 WESToN On Monday, at Ruridorn Petty Sessions' Georg,: Turner (13) erred Goorge Gordan (is) were charged with having, on the Bth December, stolen Iglbs. potatoes of the value of 6d., the property' of Wm. GrifDths, farmer, Weston. Joseph Griffiths, in the employ of the prosecutor, said in the after- noon of the day in question he saw the defendants, each with a basket in his hand, walking down a field towards several hampers of potatoes. They took a quantity of potatoes from the hampers, and placed them into their baskets. Witness then went down to them and caught Turner, who had in his basket about 2lbs. of potatoes. In Gordan's basket there Was about 10ibs. of potatoes.—The parents of the defendants !red Mr. Ford gave them leave to pick the potatoes after the plough, but the lads got into the wrong ffe-ld, and took a quantity from the baskets in mistake.—The Rev. E. A. P. Campbell said the ezcuse offered by the parents was a very plausible one, but it would net do there. The boys mast have known the difference between taking petatoes out of a hamper and taking them after the plough. For the sake of the parents the Bench would take a lenient view of the matter, and floe each de- fendant is. and costs 14s. Cd. _ _

- LEOTURE ON MkKORY AV- Ruxcoror. A large audience assembled in St. John's Presbyterian Chapel, Run- corn, en Monday evening, to listen to a lecture ion " the scien;-wonders, and religion of memory," by the Rev. Jno. Jones, formerly of itumcorn. The lecturer referred to the six divisions into vßhich the animal kingdom was divided, and dwelt upon the wonderful power of memory exhibited by some of the lower animals, mentioning par- ticularly tNe ant and the spider. He spoke of the unlimited compreherrion the human memory, if properly used, relat- ing many feats of remembrance performed by men of letters and science. The indistructilility of impressions made on the mind was shown by the narration of a number of curious facts, and the lecturer concluded a most interesting lecture by a most thoughtful exposition of the part memory- would not improbably play in the world to come. The lecture, which occupied over an hour in delivery, and abounded with facts and figures and many apposite word illustrations; was given without the aid of a single note, and at its conclusion a hearty vote of thanks was accorded the lecturer, on the motion of the Rev. J. D. Thomas, seconded by the Rev: J. Pickwell, both of whNin spoke in terms of high appreciation of Mr. Jones's performance. A similar compliment was paid to-Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst, who presided, on the motion of -the lecturer, seconded by the Rev. E. Williams.

WIDNICS STA. OF TF.IIPERANCH BRLS3 BAND. —A con- cert under the auspices of this body of instrumentalists wa3 given in Widnes Volunteer Hall, on Monday evening. There was only a moderate attendance of the public. The Rev. J. Wright-Williams presided. A programme of mis- cellaneous selections had been provided, and it was gone through with much enjoyment to the audience. The band naturally took a prominent part, and their performances I showed that skill and finish for which they have earned a reputation in local circles. Widnes Baptist choir sang several glees with good taste during the evening, Mr. Streets acting as their accompanist. Mr. G. Wright, of Earlestown, sung with his usual force and effectiveness " Man-o'•war's man," and in response to a hearty encore nave the popular song " Sailing." He also scored another success in his rendering of the " Old Brigade." The performances of 'MSS lionliton, of Runcorn, formed a pleasing part of the even- ing's entertainment, and her rendering of the songs "I may, or I may not," and "The sailor's story," were received with marked signs of approbation. Mr. I'. Davies contributed to the amusement of the audience by his comical songs, and Mrs. J. Harper and Mr. John Pownall each gave a song in good style. The solo cornet, "La Belle France," by Mr. W. Kaye. and the solo clarionette, "Corning thro' the rye," by Mr. W. Jennett, were executed in good style. The duties of accompanist were fulfilled by Mr. W. White.

A YOUNG INCORRIGIBLE AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, James Hynan, a boy ten years of was charged with stealing 3s. Oi-d. from the shop of John Mather, grocer, 36, Mersey-road, Widnes. On Monday afternoon, Elizabeth Hurst, domestic servant to Mr. Mather, examined the money drawer in the shop. It contained 3s. Id. A few minutes afterwards the prosecu- tor's young daughter Ellen saw the prisoner behind the counter near the money drawer, and she called out. Hurst entered the shop, and seeing the prisoner making his exit, she pu'rsued him but without result. It was afterwards discovered that is. (Thd. had been abstracted from the till. About eleven o'clock, on the night of the same day, P.C. Thompson apprehended the prisoner, who ad- mitted having stolen the money. It appeared from a state- ment made by Superintendent Barker, that .the prisoner had been previously convicted of stealing, and received six strokes with the biich rod. He was unmanageable, and would nol go to school his parents having been summoned before the court by the School Board nine times. He had two brothers in an industrial school, and it was a question for the decision of the Bench whether they would also com- mit the prisoner.—The Bench sentenced the boy to 14 days' imprisonment, and at the end of that period to be confined in a reformatory for five years.

IMMORALITY AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before the Rev. E. A. P. Campbell and Mr. Charles Reynolds, Peter Jones was charged, under a sum- mons, with keeping an unregistered lodging-house.—Mr. W. H. Linaker, law clerk to the Runcorn Commissioners, appeared to prosecute.—lnspector Dutton said about a quarter past one on the morning of the 14th December, he visited the defendant's house in Back Penketh-lane. He found downstairs the defendant, his wife and child, and two strange men sitting round the tire. Upstairs he found in one room a sailor and a woman of bad character, and in the same room the defendant's son and a woman.—The Chair- man: This is simply a brothel yon are keeping.—Defen- dant: No, sir.—Chairman : It is something very like it. Defendant was about to make an excuse, when the Chair- man said: At any rate you have pleaded guilty to a breach of the Lodging Clouse Act. Youwill be fined 103. and costs 9s. 6d., or, in default, 14 days' imprisonment.-31r. Linaker said proceeding in this manner was the onlr means the Board of Commissioners had of reaching this kind of cases, and he wished it to go forward to the public that in future he should ask the Bench to impose a much heavier penalty than they bad done. There were a great many complaints, not only by the police but by everybodr.—Chairman : I should -like to put a heavier penalty on this. It is quite too ' little; (to defendant) you have been let off much too cheap. —Mr. Linaker : If they get information through the news- papers that we intend to press for heavier penalties, there will be no excuse for thein.—Defendant asked for time to pay the money.—Chairman (severely) : You will have no time. You have been treated IGO leniently. If you are brought before us again you will be severely dealt with. Settle with the police at once. • CFIILnIIEN'S CONCERT AT NEWTOWN MISSION, RUNCORN. —On Wednesday evening, the children attending the New- town Mission day schools gave an entertainment of a very enjoyable character before a large audience. The Rev. T. Armson presided, and delivered an appropriate address. The programme commenced with a speech by Master Frank Littler, a boy five years of age, who showed great aptitude for his part. Miss Marlow sang "On the banks of Allan water" in a delightful manner, and "Twickenham Ferry" received a tasteful rendering from- Miss Cawley. Miss Spencer, who is a sweet singer, sang "Katie's letter ; " and Miss Marlow renewed her success in the earlier part of the evening by an excellent rendition of "Barney O'llea." The programme also included—song, "The yule log," by the children •, solo, "The busy little mother," Miss Warder; song, "Two robin red breasts ; " song, "The merry little soldier," six boys; solo, "The cobbler," Master F. Littler; recitation, "The snowstorm," Miss Wainwright; dialogue, " Miss Buxton's domestic troubles," by the teachers; song, "Cock robin," by six girls; song, "Tommy Morgan," Master Radley ; "Father Christmas," children; solo, "Wont you buy my pretty flowers," Miss Blundell; "Little newsboy,' Master F. Littler ; recitation, " Little Mary's prayer," Miss Worrell ; song, "The sick doll," four girls ; song, " Our own infant school." The children, who were conducted by Miss Biehop, the mistress, gave their several parts in a bright and tasteful manner, highly gratifying to the parents, and a vote of thanks was accorded to Miss Bishop for the able manner in which the children had been trained. Miss Bishop, who has only recently taken charge of the schools, from the Warrington Training College, shows great talent as a teacher, and will no doubt in time bring the school to a high state of efficiency. The proceeds of the ooucert were devoted to a tea party to the scholars, which was given on Thursday aftruci-;11, after blilg up for the Christmas holidays.

div.head: LOAL ARTLFIOIAL NAVIGATION. No. 11.
div.p: LOAL ARTLFIOIAL NAVIGATION. No. 11.

,r sketch of last week, we may be allowed to Cm-tinning Bay that althouvd. point of fact the Sankey Canal was the first onemade =flo. 'led in England, its being so was due p> rather to accident than The purpose of the promoters, as embodied in the Act Parliament, was to make navi- gable the Sankey Brook 0) but afterwards, on more .it carefully surveying the ground, was considered b-Ater to leave the natural bed of the streani !together, and to carry , the intended navigation as close along *he side et the stream as practicable. The powers of the p„jec:ors were enlarged by a subsequent Act of Parliament, mad On' the caal was made and fully opened in its new course in. 1700- The Bridgewater Canal follows next in order of cot, structien, and it was altogether of such unique design and purpose, being neither in the bed of any stream, nor near or parallel ; with the course of any stream but entirely across the dry land, and quite irrespective of the course of any stream except in so far as they might be made to afford supplies of water to the canal, that its claim 'to be considered the first projected canal will be at once conceded, and the Duke of Bridgewater retains his well-earned title as the "father of inland navigation in this country." Oar sketch would be incomplete were all personal reference omitted with regard to both the " Great Duke" and his engineer, James Brind- ley, the materials for which are mainly gathered from a paper contributed to the Quarterly Review by the first Earl of Ellesmere, and which we are glad to hear is in the Run- corn Free Public Libeary. The noble Earl regrets that "with the exception of -meagre articles in foreign works, no one has attempted to discharge for the Duke the task Of biography," but he fittingly adds: "The history of Francis, Duke of Bridgewater, is- engraved in intaglio on the face of the country he helped to civilize and enrich. The best records of an eminent man are certainly his works." "Francis, sixth Earl and third and last Duke of Bridge- water, was born in 1736, the youngest of five children. His father died when he was eleven years old; and one only of the four elder brothers had lived to enjoy for a short time the title. On the death of his brother, Francis succeeded to the Dukedom. Though the loss of a mother, usually a far greater misfortune than that of a father, was spared him. It is said that he met with little attention from one whose affections in the first year of her widowhood were transferred to a second husband. It is certain that his education was much neg- lected; and we have heard that some attempt was made to set him altogether aside on the score of mental deficiency." At the age of seventeen he was sent by his guardians to make the tour of Europe, having for his tutor and com- panion Mr. Robert Wood, a man of the highest distinction as a scholar, antiquarian, and traveller. Returning from his travels little is heard of him until he attained his majority, and he shortly afterwards fell in love with a young lady famous for her great beauty. The preliminaries of the mar- riage were in progress when suddenly it was broken off. The impression on the Duke was so deep, and the sacrifice so painful, that he withdrew himself from society, and is said never to have spoken to another woman in the language of gallantry. This disappoiatment in love was the crisis in his history, and at the age of twenty-two he betook himself to his Lancashire estates, and with in- domitable perseverence devoted himself to his great work, and became a benefactor to commerce, manufactures, and man- kind. His attention to his great afterwork was probably due to the knowledge that his father, the first Duke of [Bridgewater, and others, had so early as 1737, obtained an Act for rendering Worsley Brook navigable. His two chief associates were John Gilbert the land agent, and Brindley the millwridht ; the instruments for this great work being selected by Providence from the highest, the middle, and the humblest classes of society. Of these, Gilbert has naturally received scant recognition, but as accomplishing the °Mimes difficult and perplexing work of arranging terms for the land required, and raising funds with which to carry on the undertaking, he contributed no little to its success. Of Brindley little is • known, apart from his works. He was born in 1716 at Wormhill, In Derbyshire. His parents were poor, and their son en- joyed little if any educational advantages. It has even been said that he could neither read nor write; but we have seen a small book of accounts kept by him, which disproves the statement, though it bore evidences of very slender educational acquirements. At the age of 17 he apprenticed himself to a millwright in Macclesfield, and exhibited such aptitude for his trade that before the expiration of his apprenticeship, his master falling ill, he kept up the busi- ness with credit, and even supported his master and family. He afterwards established himself in business, and his local reputation became each year more ex- tensive. He had already introduced an improved method for the drainage of mines, the improvement of silk machinery, the grinding of flints, and had turned his atten- tion to the steam engine, so that it is clear that at the time he entered the Duke's service his fame as a mechanician was considerable. .He was hired at the magnificent wage of two shillings and sixpence a day, and offered to engage himself exclusively to the Duke for a guinea a week. The novelty of the projected undertaking, and, to him, the cer- tainty of its accomplishment, may hve induced him to enter the service of the Duke on these terms. Having en- tered somewhat more into detail than was our intention— but which, we elflike our readers will think at least interest- ing—we shall leave for future notice the story of the making of the Bridgewater Canal, and other information respecting it.

I have on more than one occasion commented upon the disgraceful state of Waterloo Bridge, and I was glad to see from you columns, last week, that the Runcorn Ratepayers' • Association had taken the matter in hand. The Commissioners have admitted —and who would not P—that it is in want of improve- ment by expending £3.50 in purchasing land for that putpose, and they are in possession, it is stated, of the money reqxisite for carrying out the alterations. But the torturous working of the circumlocution office described by Dickens almost pales before the circum- locution practiced by our local governors, and no doubt the plan of the work, after being bandied about on various pretexts, is lying hidden in some dusty pigeon-hole of which it has become so integral a part, that fear, almost:of desecration, will not permit it to be drawn forth. It is suprising that the main thoroughfare to the railway station should be allowed to remain without a footpath, and people are looking forward with interest to what will be the result of the association's communication to the Commis- sioners.

Widnes being so pestered with nuisances of one kind or another, of which but little notice is taken, it is refreshing to find that somebody takes so much interest in the health of the inhabitants as to try to remedy at least one. Some weeks ago, Dr. Booth called the attention of the Local Board to an escape of that vile smelling, poisonous gas, sulphuretted hydrogren from the waste heaps off Dutton-road, and an inspection by the Health Committee was pro- mised. The inspection was made and at the last meeting a reply to the complainant, tantamount to saying that no nuisance existed, was vouchsafed. Dr. Booth, conscious of the correctness of his know- ledge, waxed somewhat indignant at this, and inrormed Mr. Carey Oat he must know the gas w;u4 of a dt-leterious cbaraoter and dangerous to health. SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES.—A stonemason, named John Drummond, 53 years of age, died suddenly at tlie George Hotel, Widnes, about 11 o'clock on Tuesday morn— ing. For a period of nine years Drummond, it is stated, had suffered from heart disease and bronchitis, and he had been a patient in the hospital at Whiston Workhouse. Becoming better, he was permitted to leave the House, and Ile then came to Widnes to seek for employment. He was, however, unable to do any work, and placed himself under the care of the Union medical officer, Dr. Cooper. On Monday night he lodged at Keenaghan's lodging-house, where he was heard to cough all night. Next morning he went away without partaking of any food, and went to the George Hotel ; but he had not been there more than a few- minutes, when he was found in a recumbent position before the fire, and in a dying condition. Dr. Cooper was summoned, but the poor man was dead on his arrival.

- DEATH or MR. JonN Bastenrr, OF RONCORN.—There were interred at Runcorn Cemetery on Thursday afternoon the remains of Mr John Basnett, who died on the previous Sunday, at the age of 57, after a short illness. Mr. Basnett was tha oldest local preacher in the Runcorn circuit, 'where he possessed the power of attracting large congregations. He was greatly respected among his acquaintances, and many membrs of the Wesleyan Methodist body followed his• body to the grave. Amongst these we may mention the Revs. E. J. Robinson and George Hack, Messrs. John Simpson, T Sinister, T. Norman R. Norman, and S. Bavenscroft. Previous to leaving the chapel for the grave aide, the Rev. E. J. Robinson delivered an address, in which be earnestly exhorted his hearers to emulate the exemplary life of the deceased, mentioning the fact that on the day following that upon which Mr. Basnett died, his mother, who had been connected with the Wesleyan Connexion. since the year 1816, expired. THE ROYAL ALBERT ASYLUM FOR IDIOTS AND IMBECILES.—APPEAL. Sir,—As chairman of the Cectral Committee of the Royal Albert Asylum at Lancaster, I venture at this Christmas time to ask permission to lay before your readers a few facts with reference to the claims of that institution to the generous supped of Lancashire and the associated counties. There are at the present time 480 imbecile young persons in the asylum, of whom 223 belong to Lancashire, three being from St. Helens. For their support we depend upon payments for patients, donations and annual subscriptions to the maintenance fund, and interest and dividends arising from invested legacies. The total income from these various sources is barely sufficient for present needs, and I regret to say that we still have vacant accommodation for 120 patients. The subscribers elect a large proportion of the patients, and at every election there are many more eligible candidates that can, owing to the inadequacy of funds, be admitted. From personal observation, I can testify to the efficient and economical management of the asylum, and to the good results which have been accomplished; and I can confidently refer to the official reports of the Commissioners in Lunacy and to other impartial testimony. The Central Committee cor- dially concur with me in the desire that the vacant space may be speedily utilised to the fullest extent, and we are encouraged by the liberal support which has been accorded to us in the past. We earnestly appeal to the ladies of Lancashire to imitate the admirable example which has been set them by the ladies' association in the counties of Dur- ham and Cumberland, and in Halifax, York, Leeds, and other places. To the benevolent public of the northern counties generally, we also appeal for means to enable us to extend the benefits of the Asylum to many other families burdened with the care of helpless imbeciles who, without suitable training, are only too likely to prove life-long source of anxiety and expense to their poor relatives. I shall be glad to receive contributions; and they may also be for- warded to the general treasurers, the Lancaster Banking Company, Lancaster; or to the general secretary, Mr. James Diggens, Royal Albert Asylum, Lancaster by whom all do- nations or annual subscriptions will be promptly acknow- ledged.-1 remain, sirs, yours faithfully, WINMARLEIGH, Chairman of the Central Committee.
Winmarleigh, Garstang, Lancashire, December 16, 1882.

div.head: FARMERS' ATEETING AT THELWALL
div.p: FARMERS' ATEETING AT THELWALL

A meeting of farmers was held in the school-room, Thel- wall, on Monday evening, and was presided over by Mr. W. Darbyshire.—The CHAIRMAN read a letter from Mr. W. Royston expressing the latter's inability to be present at the meeting, and adding that he was of opinion that if the ship canal scheme could be carried out the increased water- way and the sluices necessarily provided would prevent the flooding of the whole of the Mersey valley, from which the farmers in that district had been suffering for several years. The Chairman went on to E.ty that he had a nett balance of £4 from the subscription to the fund for the prevention of floods, and he thought they could not do better than give this money to the common fund that was being raised to forward the ship canal scheme. He thought that the scheme weald be the means of preventing the floods from which they had suffered. He hoped that any of the farmers who had not subscribed would add to the amount named, and he assured them he wculd do all he could to help the scheme. Alderman Davies was there, and he had no doubt that he would show them the plans and explain matters both with regard to the carrying of manure and with regard to the prevention of the floods.—Alderman DAVIES said that Warrington and other towns had very little doubt but that the ship canal scheme would be a benefit both in a commercial and a manufacturing point of view - but perhaps the interests of the farmers 7 an- other direction. He thought that they were very properly jealous of maintaining their existing rights as to the car- riage of manure along the river, as provided by the present Navigation Act. (Hear, hear.) After making reference to the 57th clause of the ship canal Bill, he said that the weir at Howley, which was about nine feet high, would be swept away, as also would those at Thelwall, Lymm, and Mill Bank, and the whole of the river extending from Walton to Irlam would be of one uniform depth and level of surface the elevation ,being about four feet lower than the existing one; and be wished it to he clearly understood that the promoters of the ship canal did not intend to interfere with the existing river. It was their intention to put a dock at Howley.—An objection was raisect by several farmers that if the eleeation of the river was four feet lower the Woolston Cut would be drained, and then, it was asked, what would they have to do with regard to carriage of manure. They would be unable to get to the ship canal, as there would be the river between them.— Mr. Jolts; FAIRCLOVGH suggested that what the farmers would want would be the right of a wharf on the Ship Canal and a bridge across the river.—Alderman DAVIES said that it was possible the promoters of the ship canal would place a bridge across the river, and he proposed that the Chairman write Mr. Leader-Williams, the engineer, pointing out the above facts, and asking that steps be taken to admit of the farmers in that district having the same facilities for carriage as at present exist. —This was seconded hy Mr. J. HouGarroer, and carried.—Mr. CUARLES BROA.DBENT thought they would acknowledge that the ship canal would benefit the farmers in general, bat it might do a great deal of harm to particular farmers and particular interests. That being the case, it would be best to appoint a committee of the farmers in that district which was likely to be affected, to watch the progress of the pill and protest against any part of the scheme which would affect their interests. If such a deputation were to show that their farms would be injuriously interfered with, it would be sufficient to compel the promoters to make the requisite provisions against such interference or give ample compensation for the injury done. What they had to do was to make proper representations, and when the proper time came, to insist upon accommodation being made for the carrying of their manure.—A resolation was then passed that the following gentlemen he a deputation to wait upon Mr. Williams to lay their grievances before him, and ask that a clause be introduced into the bill to overcome the difficulty :—Alderman Davies, Messrs. J. Warburton, J. Houghton, T. Houghton, W. Derbyshire, and T. Bennett.— The following resolution was moved by Mr. J. HOUGHTON, and seconded by Mr. R. FAIRCLOUGH, and passed :—"That this meeting recognising the great advantages which will be conferred on this district if the praject known as the 14. Manchester Ship Canal be carried out, hereby expresses its warm approval, subject to the foregoing resolutions, and or promises to give a general support to the scherae."—A short giscussion then took place as to whether the balance of £4 should be handed over to augment the subscriptions for the err ship canal, and it was ultimately decided that the matter tPai be left until the result of the interview between the deputa- -' tion and Mr. Williams was known.—The meeting was then adjourned, on the motion of Alderman Devils, seconded by Mr. FAIRCLOUGH.—A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman, and the meeting separated.

div.head: VOLUNTEER PRIZE _DISTRIBUTION
div.p: VOLUNTEER PRIZE _DISTRIBUTION
AT LYMAI.
The annual distribution of prizes to the Lvmm Volunteer Company took place on Saturday evening last, ii the Drill Room, Lymm. The proceedings commenced with a dinner, and afterwards

Captain BOWER, commanding the company, rose to pre- sent the prizes. In doing so he congratulated them on hay- bageeacked their full strength of 100 for the first time he the life of tie company, which was now 22 years old. (Ap- plause.) They had also—for the first time in the history of the company—this year had the honour of having a member (Sergeant Rogerson) in the "Queen's Sixty." (Loud ap- plause.) But what be felt most proud of was, that again this year the company had been especially noticed by the Marshall, commanding inspecting officer, and by Colonel the battalion, for good drill, exemplary behavioar in camp, and smart soldierlike appearance on parade; indeed, the latter officer had said he considered this to be the best com- pany in the battalion. (Loud applanee.) There had been a slight improvement in the sheoting, both class firing and competitions, but the average was still below what might reasonably be expected from a company possessing, as they did, a good range close at hand. He was sorry telte was no increase in the number—which had always been small of members firing in the competitions. However, all that it might be found possible to do to remedy this uesetisfactery state of things would be done, and he hoped when they met next year they would be able to point to much greater pro- gress in shooting. (Applause.) Captain Bower then pre- sented the prizes as follow : COSMANY PRIZES. FIRST STAGE.. Colour-Sergeant Groves, £1; Sergeant W. Kirk, 155.; Lance-Corporal J. A. Thomason, 10s. 6d.; Sergeant J. Rogerson, is. 6d.; Lance- Sergeant S. Jackson, 63. ; Private F. Leah, 55.; Sergeant Niblett, ss. ; Quartermaster-sergeant Southern, 55.; Lance- Corporal G. Platt, 55.; Corporal J. Bowyer, 45.; Private P. Percival, 45.; Private J. Bell, 45.; Private G. Holt, 45.;
