div.head: WARRINGTON GRAMMAR SCHOOL,
div.p: WARRINGTON GRAMMAR SCHOOL,

DISTPABUTION OF PRIZES. The Warringto bright appearar Grammar School had an unusually ..ce on Tuesday evening, the room having been specially" which the decorated for the annual distribution of prizes took place. A large company sat down to the supper preceding the ceremony, which was performed tl bY '1" ee• P t r Stubs The chair wan taken by the headmaster, , -a Rev. E. J. Willcocks. Among the guests we noticed the Rev. Canon Heron, Mr. and Mrs. P. Stubs, Mr. and Mrs. Beamont, the Rev. and Mrs, E. C. E. Carleton, the Rev. and Mrs. S. Wilkinson, the Rev. F. W. Cory, the Rev. A. M. Mitchell, Mr. C. and Miss White, Mr. and Mrs. White, Mr. and Miss Buckton, Major Fox (of Nortt) Councillir and Mrs. Broadbent, Dr. Willeocks (of on), Mr. J. C. Thompson, Mr. G. H. l3olton, R.ev, H. a. . Smith ni\d (second master), Miss Smith, Mr. A. H. Shurrollar and Mr. Hollowell (assistant masters), dm. Abut twenty old sixth boys were present. After supper, The CHAIRMAN said: We welcome you all here to-night, and thank our friend Mr. Stubs, who, in the unavoidable Absence of Dr. Greenwood through illness, has consented to present the prizes. At the present day, when all children are compelled to attend sdtool, the subject of higher educa- tion is brought into greater prominence, and is attracting , more and more attention from those who are interested in ' the intellectual development of the youth of this country. In this direction it is our endeavour to make this school

really useful to this town and the surrounding districts. The Upper School is divided into two sides—the classical and the modern. On the former side a boy is thoroughly prepared for the learned professions and the Universities; and on the latter he receives such an education as will eminently fit him for a commercial life. It will be my aim as long as I am headmaster of this school that all boys, what- ever may be the religious creed of their parents, shall receive all the benefits of this institution without prejudice to their belief. (Hear, hear.) The school is examined annually under the Oxford and Cambridge Schools Examina- tion Board, and the report for this year—which is sixteen pages in length, and is much too long to read to you—is still more favourable than last year. The examiners in summing up say—" There is much useful work being done throughout the school, and boys are being well trained and fitted for the business of life. The boys .in the sixth form are young, but several of them are likely to do very well in a year or two's time. There are several boys of very con- siderable promise in the upper fourth form, which augurs well for the future of the school. There is a very marked improvement since last year in the style of doing the papers and in neatness, leaving in the latter point little to be desired." And let me add that much of our success is due to the hearty co-operation and effective aid of the second and other assistant masters. I conclude that We have lost one of our prizes for drawing given for several years past by Mr. Aronsberg, of Manchester, for on applying for the same last year I have had no reply; but you will be pleased to hear we have a counter-baiance from an old and valued friend, who does not forget us, and that he offers a prize to the boy who makes the best speech at our annual entertainment. When I mention this prize in connection with the name of the Rev. 0. 1:1. Cary, you will see he still retains a lively remembrance of and interest in the welfare of the old school. (Applause) I should have been glad to see the parents of the boys here to-night, but our space is limited, and I have been obliged to limit the invitations. The old sixth fellows I am always pleasd to see. The boys have been very anxious to please you this evening, and will give you a humorous dramatic entertainment prepared out of school hours for your amusement. (Applause.) Mr. P. STUBS then distributed the prizes, of which the fol- lowing is a list : CLABSICS.—VI. form, Gornall ma.; v. form, White ma.; upper iv. form, Curjel ; lower iv. form, Gornall rai ; form Reid ; ii. form, Fairclough ter.; i. form, Little- wood.
„ MATHEMATICS. VI. set, Chorley ma.; v. set, Hannah ma; upper iv. set, Kidd and Curjel, lequales ; lower iv. set, Down.

Anrrirmwric.—lll. and ii. sets, Ray mi.; upper and lower i. sets, Fairhurst. ENGLISH HISTORY, A.D. 100 G-1485. VI. and v. forms, White ma; upper and lower iv. forms, Thompson ma.; iii. and ii. forms, Ray mi.; upper and lower i forms, Row- son. _ _
—S-CIENCE.—VI. set, mechanics. &c. (a), Chorley ma.; v. set chemistry, Cawley; iv. set physical geometry, Hannah ma.
MODERN LANGUAGES.—YI. set, German, Burgess; vi. set, French, Gornall ma.; v. set German, Schonberg. DICTATION.—V. and iv. forms, Hannah ma.; and i. form', Filkin,

WRITING.-V, and iv. forms, Bowes; iii., 11., and i, forms, Fleming mi. DRAWlNG.—Shading, Chorley ma.; model, Dooley; advanced freehand, Williams ma.; elementary freehand, Dennis. MICIIARLILA TERM.—FORM PRIZES:-VI. form, Gornall ma.; v. form, Brundrett ; upper iv. form, Jackson; lower iv. form, Wheeler ma. ; iii. form Fairclongh ter.; ii. form, Littlewood ; upper i. form, Williams mi. ; lower i. form, Fox.

_ _ LATIN PROSE Plum—Hutchinson ma. ENGLISH ESSAY.—Rise and Development of the Roman Republic, Brundrett. FITCH= MARSH PRIZE.—Roman History, 133 to 50 B.C. Gornall ma. LAMPLUGH MEMORIAL.—St. Mark and St. James, with the Greek, Gornall ma. Mit.ssiNGHLaa iviEmomeir..-3t. Mark, Wheeler ma. ASHTON MEMORIAL.—SIOrrnont.

(a) Mr. Wilkinson's prize. Mr. STUBS, after distributing the prizes, said it gave him very much pleasure to be present that night, and to be able to present such a large number of prizes as he had had to present. He was very much pleased indeed to sea that there were so many boys in the school who were worthy of the prizes. (Hear, hear.) He hoped that they would continue to do well, and that they would be succeeded by others who would follow in the same steps. It seemed to him that it was not very long since he was himself a pupil, not actually in that building, but in a school almost, if not quite, on that site; but that little time was just 33 years ago this month. At that time he left the school and started out in life to do what he could, and he was very pleased with the recollection of what he saw and heard and partly learned there. He was very pleased also to find that the school was going on in mach the same lines that it went on in those days when classics formed a very important item in the education given there. He trusted that they might long continue to do so, for he really believed that for all bossiness purposes even a classical education, as far as could be given in a school of that kind to boys who left at a very early age; was about as good a foundation as could be laid for success in life. (Applause.). The first thing that was required was attention and assiduity, and, if the leaders and masters of the school were followed, that would soon be be learned there. There could be no doubt, he thought, on the part of anyone who had taken the trouble to read the reports of the examiners which had been presented to the governing body of the school from titne to time for a number of years past, that very great pains had been taken by the masters, and that great credit was due to them all. It was clear that the school bad not fallen off, in spite of increased capitation fees and -other changes—changes in the curriculum which was as good, he should think, as could possibly be provided for a school of that kind. (Ap- plause.) He again said it gave him very much pleasure to see such a large number of prizes, which he had no doubt were well deserved, and to present them in a school with which he himself was connected. (Applause.) The toast "To the memory of our founder" was then given, and drunk in silence. 11 The CHAIRMAN then proposed the healths of the gover- nors, and those gentlemen who were kind enough to give special prizes and subscribed to their University Exhibition Fund.

Mr. BnIAIONT, in responding, said it was a great pleasure to him to be present that evening. That school was founded 356 years ago, and it had had in -tlaat time 17 masters, in- cluding the present one, and including that gentleman who was mentioned in the Pincerna of last week, but whose name was mis-spelt. Well, in that 336 years there had been some most remarkable masters of the school. There were some men whose names Ought to have been handed down more than they had to posterity. There was Shaw who rescued the school when it was going to ruin, and at his own expense rebuilt the school, and commenced a suit which brought back all the property which was going from it. Then there was Hayward, a friend of Byron, the poet, and many others. Then he came down to Owen, who for 50 years was master of that school. They could see his portrait in the Warrington Art Gallery, where it deserved to be, as be was a man who really deserved well of future generations. They had had many celebrated schoolmasters, and he would remind them that the office of schoolmaster was a very important one, and one which he considered as next to the clergyman. The schoolmaster had the forming of the young mind, and it was in the form- ing of the mind that character was made. Lilly was master of that school, and afterwards of Bt. Paul's. He wag a contemporary of Aston, who taught Royalty; he taught Lady Jane Grey, and also Queen Elizabeth, so that school- masters had held high office. They had many celebrated schoolmasters, and he reminded them that Lancashire and that very neighbourhood had furnished one of the very best schoolmasters, Dr. Hornby, the present master of Eton. He did not think a better schoolmaster could be found. (Applause.) He had under his rule almost an army of scholars—a thousand, or thereabauts. Therefore he thought Dr. Hornby was a great honour to this county, and a great honour to the profession which he so well filled. As to the governors of the school, he thought they had, the interests of it at heart,, and they would see it was carried on in conformity with the rules that had been laid down. If those rules did not turn out to be as satis- factory as they might wish, the governors would do their best to make them better. He thanked them for coupling his name with the toast of the governors. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN then gave the toast "Our other guests." Mr. C. BROADBENT, who responded, said he was proud indeed to be called upon to return thanks for the visitors there that night. He thought he might say for himself and for them that there was no meeting in Warrington held dur- ing the year that they attended with greater pleasure than the annual prize-giving at the Grammar School. (Applause.) Although visitors they were most of tkem not strangers, and they took pride in the success of that school; and, what was more important, the boys took pride in it themselves. (Ap- plause.) The visitors had watched the success of that school, and it was very apparent that the boys attending there invariably improved in manner and demeanour; and that itself was of importance, as well as the other excellent teaching they got; and he argued from that that the tone of

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 23, 1882. THE DANGERS OF LEVEL CROSSINGS.

the school was very good. It would4ptrhaps, be of advantage notwithstanding that it did so well oil its present site, if the Ship Canal, of which they heard, so much, came in that direction, so that the school could be placed in the country, and be surrounded by good. playgrounds where the boys could play together, and t. tans increase the esprit de corps which already exist ir.l their school. He had very much pleasure indeed in 7:eturning thanks on behalf of the visitors, and in wishin.6,- the continuance of the success which had already mariKed the school. (Applause.) Then fol' _.oceu a dramatic entertainment:— AU 131 BA; OR, TffE FORTY THIEVES. CIIIVACTERS:-

A 1 Baba, a poor woodcutter... , Bowes, ma. Ganem, his son Reynolds, ms. Cassim Baba, brother to All Baba Chorley, ma. ii.bdalla, Captain of the Forty Thieves Hutchison, ma. Ifassarac, his rebellious lieutenant Tuckey. Mirza, one of the Forty Smethurst. Hassan, another of the Forty Grounds. Cogia Bab, wife to Ali Baba Bayley. Zaide, wife to Cassia.: Reynoldso mi. Mergiata, slave of Cassini, Carson, ma. Thieves :—Evans, Carson, ml.; Dawhurst, Cook, Wood.

SCENE I.—A FOREST.—AIi Baba, a poor woodcutter, is surprised in the forest by the Forty Thieves. He climbs a tree, and while there hears the password to their magic cAve, and wimesseslhe stabbing of Hassarac, the rebellious lieu- tenant, by his captain Abdalla, the former of whom he robs while in a fainting condition. Afterwards he enters the cave with his son Ganem.

SCENE lI.—A room in All's Cottage.—While Morgiana, the slave, is talking to Cogia, All and Ganem enter with the stolen gold. When it is discovered in their possession by Cassim, Al's brother, he compels All to tell the secret. All complies, and this concludes the scene. SCENE lll.—The Robber's Cave.—The robbers are dis- covered singing in the cave. Afterwards, when Abdalla and Hassarac are conversing, they hear someone approach- ing the case and using their password. Cassim enters, and when the robbers are about to kill him, Morgiana enters, and the robbers are all transfixed, in accordance with the words of the Enchanter of the Cave, that they were to become powerless on the entrance of any woman. Violin solo-Down.

ScENE IV.—The Verandah at All's New House.—The thieves are discovered in the jars by Morgiana, who kills them with some poison given to her by Hassarac for the purpctse of killing Ali and his family. Hassarac finds them dead in the jars, and vows vengeance. SCBNE IT.—ll ra w ing-r oo m at All's New House..—Ali, Abdalla, Cassim, Morgiana, Cianem, Cogia, and Zaide dis- covered talking. On Hassarac's fainting from the effects of poisoned lemonade given him by Morgiana, Abdalla attempts to kill All. Afterwards All pardons everyone, and the curtain falls for the last time.

The piece was well written and bristled with puns which frequently provoked the risible faculties of the audience. The young actors acquitted themselves with great credit, and some of them displayed censiderable histrionic ability. The music was selected from the "Pirates of Penzance," and was well rendered on the pianoforte by Master Downs, one of the scholars, who also gave a violin solo which was deservedly en- cored. Much pleasure was derived from the entertain ment, which it may be stated, was rehearsed on Monday afternoon in the presence of a large number of the scholars' parents and friends. The proceedings which seemed to have been thoroughly enjoyed, concluded about ten o'clock with cheers being given for the headmaster and the assistant masters of the school.

The enthusiasm which the new Ship Cf.,nal has evoked in commercial circles having extended caused the mind to turn for a tale tO the "Sankey Canal by way of antithesis. Not tq Newton, naturally Oat this was the first canal made in England by an; -- means, for the Romans, during tbele residene: en England, cut a canal from the vicinity a their tropolis, the city of York, as appears from DTake's Ebora- r bum; and in the year 1121 Henry I. made a navigable canal of seven miles in length from the Trent at Torksing to Witham in Lincoln—see Sim. Dun.; cap. 248, and the chart ef Richard of Cirencester. The Sankey Canal did not therefore give rise to the first canal navigation made in England, but qualified by the words, in modern times, the expression would be correct. An undertaking commenced in 1755, under the general powers of an Act for making navigable a river, in reality gave rise to the first canal navigation made in England. It runs entirely separate from Sankey Brook, except crossing mita mixing with it in one place about two miles from Sankey Bridges. Its length from Fidler's Ferry to the place where it separates into three branches is nine miies and a quarter. From thence it is carried to Penhy Bridge and Gerard's Bridge without going further • but from Boardman's Bridge it runs nearly to the limits of two thousand yards, making the whole dis- tance from the Mersey eleven miles and three quarters. This canal has proved very beneficial both to the public and the undertakers. Some of the first collieries upon its banks are worked out, but others have been opened, notably the Havannah collieries. Its business increased by the plate glass manufactories and chemical works founded near it in the neighbourhood of the populous town of St. Helens and formerly the large copper works belonging to the Anglesea Company, which, like Muspratt's Chemical Works at Newton, had to be 'removed and discontinued, and in passing the site of it, now occupied by the Sankey Paper Mill, now also at a standstill, we could not help thinking of the time when we saw the great chimney, 400 feet high, blown up by a company of " sappers and miners" from Liverpool, and could, in imagination, see it drop down like a huge "spill" collapsed, while thousands of people were at a respectable distance expecting it to fall endlong. How odd it is to read in the first edition of Baines' History of Lancashire, of the state of public feeling in 1824: "A new mode of conveyance, more rapid, and it is said more econo- mical than water carriage, has been instituted in some parts of this kingdom; and in the year 1822 a project was formed for constructing a railway between Liverpool and Manches- ler, on which steam-impelled carriages should travel, both with merchandise and passengers, at the rate of ten miles an hour. A number of gentlemen in Manchester and Liverpool. persuaded of the practicability of this design, entered into a subscription to defray the expenses of a survey, with a view to a parliamentary application, and the requisite sum of three hundred guineas was subscribed for the purpose. In the autumn of that year, William James, Esq., an engineer, of London, executed the survey, and suggested a line of road from Manchester by way of Eccles, Chat Moss, New Church, newton, Rainhill, Huvton, and West Derby, to Liverpool, making a distance of al miles. Public notices were accord- ingly given of an intended application to Parliament, but the measure was not followed up owing to an apprehended opposition from the whole body of inland navigation pro- prietors throughout the kingdom, and from other causes. How long these causes will operate it is difficult to say, but if, as is asserted, the conveyance of goods between the two towns of Manchester and Liverpool can by means of a rail- way, be effected at a little more than half the present charge I for water carriage, and in one-fourth of the time, the resis- tance of any body of men, however powerful, to so great a public improvement will, in the end, prove as futile as was the resistance of the land carriers I of the last age to the construction of canals." ' 'raking advantage of the fine winter's day we set out for an invigorating walk along that portion of the canal which lies in he township of Newton, and within sight of Brad- ley, described by Leland nearly three hundred and fifty years ago as" Newton on a brooke a poor market, whereof Mr. Langton hath the name of his barony. Sir Perse Lee, of Bradley, bath his place at Bradley (the moat and ancient gateway still remain), in a parke a ii. miles from Newton, and we learn that Edward the Confessor was Lord of New- ton, the barony of which passed successively to Roger de Poictou and the Langtons, and the Legh family acquired the property by purchase about two hundred awl fifty years ago—the fee of Mackerfield baing of great extent, including parts of twenty-one townships, and our authority says— " The sports of the turf and of the cock pit formerly pre- vailed in this borough to a considerable extent, but in the year 1816 they were discontinued, or rather suspended, for it is now (1824) announced that Newton races are to be re- sumed in 1825, and held this year, and in future years, the first week after Manchester races." And the next editor may add that in 1882, a new comsing ground was opened, which bids fair to take the place of the old rabbit running. For various reasons the coursing was postponed the other week till a more convenient season, and we may piously hope (" Anglo-Scotus " will lift his hands in amazement at this) that the fortunate shareholders in the new concern may not be too much downcast by their want of success so far. But as it is said," too many cooks spoil the broth," so too many of these coursing grounds diminish the chances of patronage to each, and after all, Lord Sefton does not intend to give up Altcar, any more than Mr. Legh his twenty years' contract, so the shareholders are evidently in for " a good thing " whatever their ill-wishers may say. Apropos of nothing in particular, but that we cannot resist the temptation to tell _ _

Anglo-S.cottm " through your columns that In the year 1824-5, the sum of £l4 18s. was paid, in this Newton of ours, to the mole catcher! Almost everybody in Newton has heard of or seen Castle Hill, but comparatively few know of or have seen the tumulus which is within a stone's throw of the Red House, at the bottom of Newton Common, and on the banks of the Sankey, and as far as we can see by the ordnance survey map, the only one that is on the banks of this ancient river. Being on our way,lwe turned aside to see once more this ancient burying place, and from the canal bridge at the crossing to the Havannah Collieries had a good view of this "hillock upon a mountain," as it would be called by a Celt, and wished for another "Old M.rzality," or at least an amateur photographer to preserve its outline for us, for we observe there is a trench of a yard or two in its south side to•day. It !s some 21 yards by 31 yards of an irregular slope and about three yards high, having, evidently, been explored long before the Government survey Of this part of the county was made in 1843, and we opine that this surveying party was the means of draw- ing attention to Castle Hill, not then explored, but after- wards found to be a burial place. Some may have thought we were making merry with grave matters when we sup- posed the locality already dedicated to the repose of some ancient worthy, but so it is, and "white is the world " to use the expressive phrase which in the Welsh language is

usually carved on grave stones of the mighty ded-L'and literally so to-day, though in quite another sense than that meant, for the ground is covered with snow. Making our way to Collins Green, where in passing the other day we saw that a new station was being built and a road driven under the line to do away with the level cross- ing, approaching through the fields, we notice the drainage works, which form part of the improvements, and soon after " forgather " with an intelligent stranger with whom we strike up a conversation anent these matters; and cross- ing the line find' ourselves standing beside the barricade fencing off the new cutting, and remarking upon the diffel•ent appearance of a finished and unfinished piece of work, upon the greater knowledge and skill of civil engineers now than formerly, and which makes them demand better work of contractors. Of the really good work put into Earlestown bridge by Mr. Fisher, who is also the contractor for this new piece of work, which seem most satisfactory so far. That a new house is to be built where , the old station is. That one of the signal b6xes is to be done away with, along with the present road, and that a grand new hotel is to be built near where the Pear Tree public-house is, of which the proportions are to be something handsome, and the accommodation ample; and the expense adequate to the means of Sir Gilbert Greenall—a sum we hesitate to msntion out of deference to our friends of temperance--so far so good. When the signal man sung out "Look out," and our new friend said quietly "Your dog is done for," for he was on the track, just at our heels. In an instant we stretched out our hands and grasped him, stepping on to the track while doing so, when we saw the Manchester express clearing the nine arches, and in less time than it takes to tell were holding on our hat to withstand the wind caused by the rush which the train brought up with it. Our friend looked a moment, and then said, "You nearly lost your life because of your love for your dog," and we thought "that" is another example of . the dangers of a level crossing, and brought to mind the action of a relative of ours, who, seeing a man on the track of an express, flung herself at him, and threw him into the six-foot. That was esteemed an act of bravery, and so rewarded—this an act of folly; so differently are things regarded by some people. Conversation turned on the state of the nine arches, which we thought, in pass- ing under them safe enough, and so they are with this slight defect, that the foundations have shifted, and so the superstructure is slightly out of " plim," an expressive phrase which means that, like a drunken man, it is just a little out of the perpendittular. and may some fine day descend to the level of the Sankey, over which it proudly sits, and a picturesque object in the landscape.

THE NSW ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY.—It is announced that the Queen has offered the vacant Archbishopric of Canterbury to the Right Rev. Dr. Benson, Bishop of Truro, and that his Lordship has accepted the post. The Right Rev. Edward White Benson, D.D., who is of a Yorkshire family, was born near Birmingham, in 1829, and is, there- fore, in his fifty-third year. He was educated at King Edward's School, Birmingham, and at Trinity College, Cambridge, of which he was successively a scholar and Fellow. He graduated B.A. in 1852, when he was Senior Chancellor's medallist, a senior optime, and first-class in the classical tripos. He tOok holy orders in 1853, and was for some years examining chaplain to the Bishop of Lin- coln. He was for some years assistant master at Rugby, and was head master of Wellington College from its first opening in 1858 to 1872, when he was appointed a Canon Residentiary and Chancellor of Lincoln Cathedral. In December, 1879, he was nominated by the Crown on the recommendation of Lord Beaconsfield to the newly created Bishopric of Truro taken out of the diocese of Exeter, and was consecrated at St. Paul's Cathedral on April 25, 1877. Dr. Benson married in 1859, Marv, daughter of the late Rev. William Sidgwick, of Skipton, Yorkshire. KAY'S TIC Plats, a specific in Neuralgia. Face-ache, &e, 91(1, 1s 10d; postage Id. ANOTHER COLLIERS' D,ISPUTII.O HAYDOCK. MEETING OF THE MEN. During the past few 'neits a dispute of an 'annsual character has arisn between the firm of Mesars. Richard Evans and ',do., of the Haydock, Ashton, and Go'borne c°,l.lries, and a proportion of the hands employed by them. It is stated that about three weeks ago three men, members of the local branch of the Miners' Society, received notice to leave, and as these men took an especial interest in the late dispute and acted as leaders, it was thought by many that the firm were thus retaliating upon the men. The latter, however, were far-from being disposed to seeing their leaders thus thrown out work, and the matter was frequently dis- cussed. Ultimately a deputation waited upon Mr. B. B. I Glover, the agent of the firm, and the interview took place on Saturday forenoon last. As a result it was ascertained that Mr. Glover knew nothing about the matter, and that it rested with the manager of one of the pits. For the purpose of hearing the result of the interview, and of deciding upon some future course of action a mass meeting of the men was called for the same afternoon on Ashton Heath. Considering the very unfavourable weather, there was a good attendance of miners. Instead, however, of holding the meeting in the open air, it was thought advis- able to adjourn to the Fleece Inn, Ashton in the large room of which the business was transacted, there being a crowded attendance. Amongst those present were a number of females-who were out on "strike," as the firm of Messrs. Evans refused to grant them an advance of wages. Mr. SAMUEL WOODS, of Park-lane, presided, and in addressing the meeting he said he was sorry that any grievance should arise in that district about which they had seen Mr. Glover that morning. He thought after such a very long and hard struggle as they had had that they would have had peace for a long time to come. However, it appeared that little evils kept cropping up in one corner and then another. At the same time nearly everything they had to complain about came from one source. They were not going to blame anyone not responsible for the men being victimised, and they were not going to lay the blame upon I any person who was not guilty of it. He did not believe , Mr. Glover was guilty, but it was Mr. Cooke, manager at the I Ram Collie, who was solely to blame for the present evils that had called them together. He alluded to the difficulties under which the check-weigher at the Ram pit laboured, and stated that the matter had been reported to Mr. Hall, the Government Inspector of Mines for the district, and he (Mr. .Woods) had also written to Mr. Glover about it, stating that the check-weigher had not the facilities afforded to him which he ought to have by At of Parliament, namely, that he could not see the machine from the place where he was in the weighing place, and further, that the manager was constantly in the habit of going in the machine place and tampering with the machines, threatening the check-weighers, /Lc. He thought Mr. Glover ought to have stopped the manager for unduly using his authority—(" So he ought.")—and then, probably, there would have been no reason for them to assemble there. The matter was reported to the miners' delegates at their district meeting, and he (Mr. Woods) was appointed to write to Mr. Hall, stating the facts of the case, which he did. From what he knew of Mr. Hall, he thought he was a gentleman who would do his duty, and he believed he had done it in that case. He wrote back to him (Mr. Woods) reporting the result of his visit to the colliery. He had forced them to alter the machine which he considered most unfair. As he had just said, all the evils sprang from one source—from one man in the whole of the collieries—one manager out of the large number of managers employed by the firm, who was self-willed, wanted his own way in everything, and did not consider the interests and rights of the men, but they were so united that they were determined to have the evils uprooted and have fair play in future. (Hear, heat.) He thought it was very unrea- sonable for any body of workingmen to have such a manager, and he thought there was nothing wrong in the course the men had pursued. The manager referred to said, "I will try to upset that society," and picked out two or three of their members. He (Mr. Woods) ventured to say that one of the men was the quietest in Haydock, and most unlikely to do anything unreasonable or anything that would get him his discharge. The body of men under their firm aad 11 the Federation of Lancashire felt keenly on the matter, and they were not going to allow any member of their associa- tion to be put on either by master or manager. All they wanted was fair play. Seeing that they had got so far as the 19th century they thought that tyranny was a thing that ought to die out—(hear, hear)—and it should not be exercised. A deputation had been to Mr. Glover that morn- ing, and they had four questions to ask him. The first was " What have you discharged these men for—what have they done amiss ?" Mr. Glover said he did not actually know the men were discharged. He (Mr. Woods) believed that as a rule it was not the agent but the managers who took upon themselves to bring about disputes and grievances in the collieries. The second question was " How is it these men who have been discharged cannot have a place of work under this firm?" One of. the men had got work at another place under the firm, but had since been stopped. Mr. Glover denied it. The next question came, "Why should Mr. Cooke say that there will not be a man under that firm if he ie in the society in six months ?" Mr. Glover treated the matter as wind, and said that the men had a perfect right to organise themselves so long as their organisation was legitimate and carried on in a legal man- ner. The next question was, "What about these men starting ?" Mr. glover said they ought to be allowed to start anywhere under the firm. He was not going to in- struct his managers to take any unjust advantage of the _men • and one manager in the room said he would fin of the men a place himself. He had a resolution to pro- pose—" That this meeting is of opinion that the recommen- dation of the deputation be accepted, namely, to recommend the men affected to seek ernployment from the other managers under the firm, seeing that Mr. Glover promises not to use any influence against the men on account of their being connected with the miners' society, and pledges itself to act together if they are not found proper places of work."—A COLLIER seconded the resolution, which was carried unanimously.—Mr. JOHN CROSS (St. Helens) then addressed the meeting, observing that the discharge of the men was no new grievance—it was the old tactics of the ignorant managers of some years back. Mr. Cooke tried to do something by discharging two of their members of society, but were they going to allow him to take that advantage of their leaders? ("No.") If they allowed him to take advantage of their prominent members they weie cowards, and were not worthy of being called Englishmen. (Applause.) He alluded to the case of the " brow girls," who Were out on strike, as the firm would not give them an advance of wages, and asked the men to assist in supporting them.—lt was afterwards decided that the men should pay a small sum per week towards the support of the girls on strike, and the meeting concluded.

THE PERILS or CURIOSITY. At Hammersmith, on Tuesday, Robert Rymill, a carman, was charged with steal- ing two diamond rings, value £2O, the property of Mrs. Edith Browning, of Redcliffe-street, South Kensington. The prosecutrix said that on Saturday evening the prisoner came to the house with some goods from the stores. She asked him to place them on the dresser. She left him alone while she drew some ale, which he drank, and after he was paid he left. Ten minutes afterwards she missed the rings,which she had left on the dresser shelf. Rymill said he had no intention to steal the rings. He took them to look at and had not time to put them back, as the lady came in, and he put them into his pocket, intending to return them. Having pleaded guilty, Mr. Sheil committed him to prison for three months with hard labour. div.head: WARRINGTON SAVINGS' BANK.
div.p: WARRINGTON SAVINGS' BANK.
ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting in connection with Warrington Savings' Bank was held at the Bank, Buttermarket-street, on Tuesday morning. The Ex-Mayor (Alderman Picknaere) presided,and there were also present Messrs. W. Long, F. Monks, J. Davies, J. White, T. Jolley, Rev. A. Kenworthy, C. Broadbent4W. Darbyshire, J. Woolfall, and J. E. Davies (actuary). The CHAIRMAN, in moving that the statement of accounts as prepared by the actuary and examined by the account- ant, be approved, and that one copy be transmitted to the National Debt Commissioners, and a duplicate be publicly affixed at the Savings' Bank, said they would observe that the bank funds were gradually increasing year after year. If they would look at the comparative statement of the business of the institution they would see that in the last 12 years the number of accounts had increased from 6,035 to 8,912, and the balance due to depositors from £210,000 to £273,000. He thought that showed the bank was doing a great deal of good, that it was carried on in a proper manner, and that the public thought so. Mr. LONG seconded the motion, and referred to a sugges- tion that had been made in committee, and that he thought would work well, that they might attend at the public schools in town to receive deposits from the children. He heard that that had been largely done in some towns, and had formed a feeder as it were to the banks, by inculcating in the children the habit of saying. The committee of the bank were anxbus in every way to increase the facilities of the bank. After a little conversation,

The CHAIRMAN said the point was this: they had got a clerk whose time was not fully occupied, and Mr. Long thought he might go round to specified schools, and see if he could get them to adopt some means whereby he cculd receive money at a certain time and induce the children to invest in the bank. Mr. Loma said he had spoken to one of the managers of a large school, and he seemed to think it would be a very good thing. Alderman DAVIES said the clerk could not receive money, as the rules would not allow him.
The CHAIRMAN said they would be merely sending him round to assist the managers of schools.
Ile motion was carried.
ANNUAL REPORT.

The annual report of the committee of management was as follows :—The committee of management has pleasure in submitting the general statement of the funds of the bank far the year ending 20th November, 1882. The total funds amount to £275,497 4s. Bd., as under: With the National Debt Commissioners on general account, £272,104 Os. 7d. ; on separate surplus fund account, £700; and the balance in the ban is of the treasurer is £2,603 4s. 1.; total, £275,497 4s. Bd. £7,140 Os. 74 interest, and £l6 13s. Od. dividends on stock have been credited depositors during the year, and the total amount due to them is £273,621 Sc. Od., showing an increase of £2,249 17s. 9d. 824 new accounts have been opened, and 692 closed, showing an increase for the year of 132. The total number of depositors, including friendly and charitable societies and penny banks, now is 8,942. As many as 8,658 deposits have been made during the year, and 5,314 payments. At the monthly meetings of the com- mittee the accounts of the institution have been examined and found correct. It is a pleasure to present so satisfac- tory a report, especially as to the increase in number of accounts, the total number now approaching nine thousand, showier"' that the institution is doing good work. No one knows better than those who have experienced it, how pleasant and easy it is to lead provident lives, and save up for a rainy day, and the committee hope that the depositors will read this report, and hand it on to some friend or neigh- bour with a word of encouragement to make a beginning. The money deposited is theirs, but in safe keeping, anti always ready for them when wanted. There are many now with large sums to their credit who bless the day they started to save with a few pounds or a few shillings. Sums as low as one shilling are received, and children over seven years of age may themselves come to the bank and open accounts. Parents should encourage their children in provi- dent habits, and they cannot do better than send, and assist them, to deposit their savings. It becomes a habit to a many, and a pleasure to come to the bank, and no one can make a commencement too early life. For those who can- not attend in the working hours 'of the day, the bank is open on Saturday evenings, and it is gratifying ba see that the numbers availing themselves of this privilege are in- creasing.—For the committee of management, Joule RD. PICIMERE, chairman; WM. LONG; vice-chairman. Mr. DARERSHIRE proposed that the report of the Com- mittee of Management be approved, and that the meeting acknowledged the valuable services rendered to the insti- . _

tution by the gentlemen acting on the committee during the past year, and tendered its best thanks to them.. Mr. BROADBENT seconded the proposition which was agreel,to. On the motion of Mr. MONKS, seconded by Mr. T. JOLLEY, Alderman Pickmere was re-elected chairman, and Mr. Wm. Long ice-chairman. The CHAIRMAN in reply, said they were surrounded by a staff of officials who made their work very easy. He believed honestly that with the assistance of the very good committee which they had the bank was thoroughly man- aged, and on the best principles. Mr. LONG also, expressed his thanks for the confidence they had reposed in him. _ _

Alderman DAVIES proposed, Mr. JOHN WHITE seconded, and it was agreed that the Committee of Management con- sist of the following :—Chairman, vice-chairman, Messrs. S. Rigby. F. Monks, John White and Joseph Davies, trustees; Messrs. T. Jolley, J. Wootton, Wm. Qwen; junr., S. Lees, J. Smethurst, Rev. J. Yonge' W. Darbyshire, J. K. Young, James Morris, and the Rey. A. Kenworthy. After other formal business had been disposed of, the meeting concluded with a vote of thanks to the chairman.

The reason why so many are unable to take Cocoa is that the varieties commonly sold are mixed with starch, under the plea of rendering thefts soluble; while really making them thick, heavy, and indigestible. This may be easily detected, for if Cocoa thickens in the cup it proves the addition of starch. Cadbury's Cocoa Essence is genuine; it is therefore three tirnes the strength of these Cocoas, and a refreshing .beverage like tea or coffee.-4dvt.

div.head: SHOCKING DEITH ON THE RAIL-
div.p: SHOCKING DEITH ON THE RAIL-

WAY AT ST. HELENS. A BRAKESMAN NEARLY CUT IN TWO: On Thursday afternoon, John James Penning(Oti, 24 years of age, who was employed by the London and North' Western Railway Company as a brakesman, met with a shocking death on the Eccleston branch, near St. Helens. This branch is used exclusively for goods and mineral tragic. It leaves the main line near Raven-street Bridge and terminates—one section at the Ravenhead Glass Worke and the other near Eccleston Church. It was constructed for the convenience of the large Crown Glass Works of Messrs. Pilkington Brothers, the Greenbank Alkali Cora- pany, the St. Helens Collieries, and numerous other worki in the vicinity. The system of rails is necessarily very CO plicated on account of the many sidings, and heavy traffic, and accidents there have been frequent. It apPearS that to a great extent waggons are pushed, and not drawn, up these branch lines, so that the engines are invariably at the end of the train nearest to the main line. On Thurs- day a number of trucks laden with slack were being pushed towards Ravenhead, and deceased and another of the cora' pany's servants were sitting on the front waggon. WheS,, approaching Messrs. Pilkington's siding they noticed the the facing points were only half closed, and knowing that an accident must occur when the wheels struck the point Pennington's companion jumped off and got clear. It dee not seem certain what movement Pennington made, but Oa reaching the points the first and second waggons were over' turned and several others left the rails. Deceased was thee noticed to be lying across the metals, having been run oval by two waggons. One of Messrs. Pilkington's Tee° hastened to his assistance, and tried to lift him up, but was horrified to find that deceased was nearly cut in two, and that his internal parts dropped out. THE FOOTPATH NEAR BROOKSIDE MILLS, StO. With reference to the footpath ,near Brookside M" which has been several times considered by the committee, the Surveyor handed in the following report :—" I inform you that Mr. J. E. Pardev has made arrangelnee"; with me to construct the new footbridge and footpaths nt Brookside Mill, and the work on the ground will be Put hand as soon as the weather is favourable. Mr. Jute, 7 Wakefield is already preparing the woodwork for the brig:. The footpath running parallel with the brook from Parp. side Mill to Brookside Mill has been repaired in accordance with the instructions received at the last meeting. 111! work ordered to be done at the sewerage outfall has been 36: tended to. The water rents laid on the new assessment anaonfr: to Di 10s. per quarter more than on the old assessment, I have prepared an estimate for laying a three inch wate` main from Mr. John Bate's, Brickmakers' Arms, to )fre* Alice Hague's, Edge Green-lane. There are 20 houses alai the road between these points without a supply of goo" water, and the water rents from them would amount to 13s. 4d. Mr. George Holme, county surveyor, inspect_ the road (which we petitioned the County Authority t`' declare a main road) on the 14th ult., previous to repeal upon it to the County Highway Committee. M. 1,1°1°) considered that the railway station was the princiPet ,ture in . our application. Since his visit I ha7e De, received any communication as to whether the road by been adopted."

div.p: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY Ci iMMITTEE. The monthly meeting WAS held in the Commissioners' Beard-room, on Tuesday. The Rev. Canon Barclay pre- sided, and there were else present Dr. MacDougall, Dr. Steele Messrs. John Simpson, F. Lake, W. Rhodes, Wm. Handley, J. R. Frith, P. Briscoe, Riley, and We Brookes (secretary). LTERAMIAN'S REPORT. Mr. J. D. JONES, the librarian' reported that 1,558 books had been borrowed feom the lending 'library during the month of November. They were classified as folloes : Theology, 33: philesophy, political economy, and law, 12; history, travels, add biography, 267 ; science and art, 10; poetry and the drama, 32; prose and fiction, 1,026; miscel- laneous, 108. 'During the month £1 Os. 3d. had been re- ceived for fines; other receipts bringing the total to us. U. A number of volumes had also been presented, and it Was decided that the customary -ecknowledgement should be lorwarde,d on the motion of Dr. MACDOUGALL, seconded by 4e. BEISCON. MR. HAZLEHURST'S OFFER ACCEPTED. Mr. Eft OOLIth read the resolution from the ratepayers' -meeting 'referred to the Committee by the Comnaissioners, and which thought it was the opinion of the meeting that a reading room and free -library should b 3 opened at Waterloe Hbuse.—Dr. STEELE -remarked that the resolution wee re- ferred to the Committee because the Board of Commissioners 'thought they had Yietually nothing to do with the matter.— ' DreltacDonnam traced the circumstances attending Mr. Hazlehurst's offer from the commencement, and -said Mr. liazlehurst was in attendance on the Committee to explain • the scheme which he individually wished to promote in the interests of the working classes, and for the classes ' for whom tine Library was especially established. 'Mr. Hazlehuref's scheme was one which the committee would have no difficulty in accepting. Many of the mem- bers had thought that they could not -'support a scheme for the establishment of a reading-room, if the-reading-room were to be supplied with daily newspapers, but Mr. Hazle- hurst only intended that weekly and monthly periodicals, and the bueks in the library, should be provided, and he was prepared to defray the whole cost for three years not only of the supply of these periodicals, but of fitting up the room at Waterloo House. He (Dr. MacDougall) thought the committee would scarcely be doing right if they stepped in beteessen Mr. Haziehurst and the ratepayers, or at all events"the reading community, in a thing of this kind. It seemed to him to be the duty of the committee to give effect to Metazlehurst's wish in the matter, inasmuch as be did not ask them to incur one penny of cost, he himself being prepared to pay all expenses in connection with the reading- -room. Mr. Hazlehurst had undoubtedly changed his views, and-he (Dr. MacDougall) thought all credit was due to him for leaving done so. He hoped there would be no divided ' 'opinion on the subject, which they were in a position to discuss clearly.—Mr. W. HANDLEY saki he should like to correct one statement made by Dr. MacDougall. Dr. Mac- Dougall stated that Mr. Hazlehurst had modified his scheme ft•Om a news-room to a reading-room. It seemed that every- one had misapprehended- Mr. Hazlehurst's meaniag from the first to now. He did not intend to establish anything further than a reading-room, where people could quietly t read books from the library and weekly papers - and magazines. It had never been Mr. Hazle- hurst's intention to have a daily news-room. • The CHAIRMAN: Mr. Hazlehurst had better explain his own - scheme. Is it your wish that Mr. Hazlehurst be admitted to explain the scheme P—On the motion of Mr. LAKE, seconded by Dr. STEELE, Mr. Hazlehurst was requested to - appear before the committee, and he did so.—Mr. Lexe said it would, perhaps, be the simplest course if he were to read what he had put down- as Mr. Hazlehurst's scheme. He un- derstood it to be as follows:—(1) To entirely furnish the ' reading-room, including tables, chairs, gas fittings, floor • cover, and other requisites. (2) For three years to provide ' illustrated and other weekly papers at e monthly magazines according to the selection of this committee. (3) To pay any additional expense for librarian or assistant's salary, owing to the rooms being open six nights a week instead of three as at present. (4) The above arrangements and the management of the reading-room to be under the entire con- trol of the committee.—Mr. HAZLEHURST : That is exactly my offer, Mr. Chairman. (Applause.)—Dr. STEELS was sure that they were all greatly indebted to Mr. Hazlehurst for his munificent offer, and he begged to move that it be accepted, subject to their first ascertaining whether the committee could rent such rooms as they required from the Commis- sioners. He thought a rent of £2O a year would be sufficient ferthe rooms the committee would require. If the Com- missioners also removed to Waterloo House the spare rooms could be let off as offices in any way the Board might entertain. The CHAIRMAN : Do you know if we have power to rent a room ? Dr. STEELE: Oh, yes; I think so.—Mr. RHODES said he thought it would be best to leave the question of rent in - abeyance, observing that if the Commissioners took rent, they were preventing the committee from attaining what"' was really their object—a useful and extensive library.— Dr. STEEL remarked that by the Library Act the Commis- sinners were not empowered to spend more than a penny in the pound. That full penny they gave the Library Com- mittee, and out of that the committee ought to pay rent.— Mr. Farm understood that the Commissioners had to pro- vide the Library Committee with rooms free of charge.— Mr. HANDLEY said the Commissioners could not charge • rent. If they could, they would have to hand over the rent they charged to the Library Committee. It was so stated in the Act of Parliament. The Commissioners' only power was to provide rooms for the Library Committee. If the Commissioners bad no spare rooms they could allow ' Library Committee to provide them for the use of the town with the consent of Her Majesty's Treasurer. There was no such thing as rent mentioned in the Libraries Acts. The whole extent and construction of the Acts went to show that rent could not be charged. If the Library Committee required rooms, and the Commissioners had no rooms, then they would have power to erect or rent rooms, but only in that case. That expense would then be the first charge upon the Library rate; but so long as the governing body had rooms it was bound to allow the use of them for the purposes of a library. Dr. STEELE begged to differ with Mr. Handley, remarking that he should take advice on the question. He only wanted to do what was right and proper. He would take the trouble to write to the auditor, who, no doubt, would explain the matter fully.—Mr. LAYS remarked that this discussion was irregular, and moved "This committee having con- sidered the resolution passed at a ratepayers' meeting, held on the sth inst., and haying heard Mr. Hazlehurst's explana- tion of his offer, most strongly recommends the acceptance of Mr. Hazlehurst's munificent offer, and that such resolu- tion be carried into effect without delay."—Mr. HANDLEY said he had great pleasure in seconding the motion. He thought it was stated by Sir James Picton when the library was opened that a public library had a „wonderful power of attracting gifts to itself. They had scarcely had a monthly meeting, but there had been something great or small given to the library, and this the latest of all, was the most munificent gift that they had had yet. It was the gift to the town of a considerable sum ef money for intellectual purposes, and its results could scareely be calculated at present.—Mr. Leis observed that Mr. Hazlehurst was per- fectly willing to give any guarantee or sign any document which might be thought advisable, to find furniture and books for the next three years, and to indemnify the library committee from any expense. (Applause.)—The CHAIR- MAN observed that the committee had not power to carry the resolution into effect, and Dr. STEELE said the Commis- sioners were of opinion they had not. Let the committee get rooms from the Commissioners and then they (the committee, would carry it out. At the suggestion of the Chairman, who said he wished to send the resolution to the Commissioners in a res- pectful manner, the words " that the Commissioners be respectfully requested" were added to the resolution, which was carried unanimously.—Dr. STEELE then moved • "That this committee respectfully requests- the Commis- • aioners to grant for the use of the library and reading-room, the breakfast, dining, and drawing-rooms of Waterloo • House, and to empower the committee to make and carry out the necessary arrangements."—Mr. RHODES seconded the resolution, which was carried. MR. HAELERCRST'S RESIGNATION. Mr. Farm proposed a resolution to the effect that the committee considered it advisable to continue Mr.tiazlehnrst a member of the Library Committee, and that such altera- tions be made in its constitution as might be necessary. He thought after the interest Mr. Hazlehurst had shown in the library, from its commencement up to the present, they would greatly miss his services at the present time, and he was sure the Commissioners would think with the commit- tee, thatit would be advisable to continue him a member.— The Cereanareie : As soon as a vacancy occurs.—Mr. Hem:omit : There is a vacancy now.—Mr. FRITH said, as at present arranged, Mr. Hazlehurst-could not sit as an outside member,, but the Commissioners could make an alteration in 'the arrangement so as to enable him to come in.—Dr. STEELS, said he was very sorry that Mr. Hazlehurst was not a member of the Library Committee. The constitu- tion of the committee, however, could not be altered without rescinding a resolution, and for various . reasons he could net recommend that course.— Dr. MAcDocciahe thought Dr. Steele quite right. He was in • 'avow: of the committee as at present constituted. In due -course a vacancy would occur, and there could be no two opinions that Mr. Hazlehurst would be entitled to the place, and would be put upen the committee. He should be glad, awl no deubt the ratepayers would be equally gild, when :that time arrived. efore the committee separated, they ,-eught to pass a resolution thanking Mr. Hazlehurst for his Ammediageysenerous offer, and put it upon the tecords of -the committee. He regretted that Mr. Hazlehurst was no longer a InemLer of the committee, and hoped the thne would speedily come when he would be able to join them , again. The committee ought to take some formal notice of Mr. Hazlehurst's offer, becaute he had certainly granted to them—he really clid not know how to express himself—but it was something very munificent inieed.---Mr. BRISCOE seconded Mr. Frith's relation. If the Commissioners could see their way to grant the request, ae should be glad to see Mr. Harleburst again on the committee. It wee an honour which he highly deserved.—Dr. STErhs remarked upon the antagonistic character of the resolution, and said it would not be wise to alter the constitution of the committee.—Mr. Farm said he was sorry that any resolution proposed by a member of the committee shoultl be thought to be antago- nistic to the Commissioners. The committee was appointed for the welfare of the Library • it was for the members to look out for the best means of carrying on the Library effectively; and he thought after what Mr. Hazlehurst had done, it was only right for them to expect that his zervices would be a great boon to tho Library Committee. There- fore they were natitrally anxious to get him on the ponizaittee, and he OIL Fritb) did not think the Com-

missioners would be at all antagonistic on tilts question.— The CHAIRMAN : But your resolution wC)uld alter their standing orders, and if I were the Contrnissioners I would not do it.—Mr. LIKE said there were certainly great objec- tions to altering the standing orders.—Mr. RILEY asked if it would be any advantage if he were to retire from the committee in favour of Mr. Haztuauits'r.—Mr. SIMPSON thought it would be a great mistake to ask the Commis- sioners to alter their standing orders.—Mr, PRIM taid under the circumstances he would withdraw his promsition, and he seconded Dr. I.acDougall's vote of tharAlo to Mr. Hazle- hurst.—The motion was carried unanimously.—Dr. STEELE asked a queetion with reference to the tatter from Mr. Hazlehurst, read at the last meeting of the committee, the consideration of which was postponed.--]r. MacDouqat.t. said he was authorised to state that the letter was with- drawn.—This was the whole business.,

BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVE- MENT CLASS, RUNCORN. The members of the Brunswick Mutual Te.Vrovement Class on Wednesday night celebrated the twentieth anniver- sary of the tiess, the gatherins- being one of the most suc- cessful evet held in connectic-a with the society. Meeting at half-pet six o'clock, at the Brunswick schoolroom about sixty sat down to a tea well prepared by 'Mr. and Mrs. Molyner.x. Tea over, the members adjorried to one of the large vestries, and the meeting for the transaction of busi- ness was at once held. The President was in the chair, and among those present were several Elf' the vice-presidents and committee, and tlee secretaries.—Mr. F. J. Norman, sec- retary, read the report, which stated that the past year had been an eminently satisfactory one, and it might safely be asserted that never before had etch excellent papers gone to make 'up the programme of any segsion. It was with the profoundest regret the committee recorded the lots by death of Mr. A: E. Littler, a young but worthy member of the class, and that of Mr. Charles Soulby, Iwho, as a member, and afterwards as a vice-president, had I rendered signal service in the interests of the class. The ' session bad been made up of 44 meetings, 16 of which were devoted to Bible studies, three to readings by members, three to impromptu speaking, and 22 to lectures, essays, kc. In conclusion, the committee reminded them that the success of the class depended for the most part on the individual ' efforts of the members, And they sincerely hoped that with I, this co-operation the forthcoming year would be more suc- cessful than any that had preceded it. The repott having been unanimously adopted, the meeting proceeded to the re-election of presi lent. Mr. Kniveton, in well-chosen terms, referred to the long connection of Mr. Simister as president, and they could not now afford to dispense with his services. It was, therefore, with the utmost pleasure that he moved his re-appointment; and that he be thanked for his past services. The motion was ably supported, and unanimously carried. Mr. Simister briefly returned thanks. Votes of thanks were passed to the vice-presidents, and they were re-elected with the exception of the Revs. E. J. Robinson andiS. Ylees, who were elected in the place of the Revs. J. Nowell and J. Bateman. The secretaries, Messrs. F. J. and A. R. Norman were cordially thanked and re- elected. The committee was also re-elected. The rest of the evening was spent in a very interesting manner, songs and readings being given by members and a few short addresses by members of the class.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. E. BILLINGSLEY, OF RUNCORN.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. E. BILLINGSLEY, OF RUNCORN.

It is with great regret that we record the death of Mr Elijah Billingsley, which took place at his residence Duke's Field, Runcorn, about two o'clock yesterday (Friday) morning. Mr. Billingsley, who had only attained the age of 31, had suffered for some weeks back from a severe cold, caught luring a drive from Norley to Runcorn in a heavy rain, and on Tuesday last he became so unwell that the a.tendance of a medical man was necessary. Dr. Mouritz was called in and pronounced his patient to be suffering from a lacerated throat and inflammation. During the fol- lowing two days the symptoms assumed alarming propor- tiens, and Dr. Glyn, of Liverpool, was called into consulta- tion on Thursday evening. No hope of recovery was held out, ind Mr. Billingsley sank rapidly, and died as stated. Mr. Billingsley, who was a native of Runcorn, was a prominent member of the Primitive Methodist body in the town, and he was ever active in promoting every good objtct in connection therewith. He had the cause thoroughly at heart, and no labour was toe arduous if he thought he could thereby advance it in any degree. His position as organist in the chapel he took advantage of to raise money to add to the funds, which of no place of worship are ever too large, doing this by means of concerts, &c. In February last, he produced a service of song, eptitled "The basket of flowers," which he had himself composed, and which achieved considerable popularity. • About three weeks ago, he conducted a successful perfor- mance of it in Warrington. We understand that Mr. Bil- lingsley had also composed another service of song, which is in the hands of the printer, and it is a melancholy thought that he will not have the gratification of hearing it performed ; but as one of his latest efforts in music, a which he was very fond, it will be a memorial to his family and friends of his ever active spirit and kind philan- thropy. For he did not confine his good deeds to one de- nomination, other churches frequently receiving his wel- 'come aid. For a. considerable number of years, and at his death, Mr. Billingsley occupied the onerous post of chief clerk and cashier at Mr. Timmin's ironfoundry, and yester- day a lag was flying at half-mast over the scene of his
Mr. Billingsley leaves- a wife and four children to mourn his loss.

WARRINGTON SCHOOL OF SCIENCE. ADDRESS BY MR. THOMAS MORRIS. On Saturday evening last Mr. Thomas Morris, manager for Messrs. Pearson, Knowles, and Co.. Limited, addressed the pupils of the Iron and Steel Classes connected with the Warrington School of Science. In the course of his remarks, Mr. Morris spoke Ist, on fluxes for smelting iron ; 2nd, on the puddling process and production of grains of iron; 3rd, on the development of fibre from the grains. The principal flux used by the smelter of iron is carbonate of lime. Some limestones are very .full of fossils, and these often contain a largo amount of phosphoric acidiand iron pyrites. Such limestones are avoided owing to those deleterious substances. Iron at all temperatures above the red heat has an affinity for phosphorous and sulphur, the phosphorous causing what is known as "told shortness." The sulphur, which is a large component in the pyrites, causing what is known as hot or red shortness, i.e., the iron will not bend to the blacksmith's designs without cracking if he works it at red heat, as be has to do in making a horse shoe. Neither are the dolomitic or the magnesian limestones so useful as the more pure cal- carons varieties, owing to the Magnesia diminishing the fusibility. You will readily understand that the flux which does not fuse quickly, will cause waste of iron. I Limestone, in contact with the earthly matter that forms part of the argillaceous ironstones, melts as easily almost As lead in a cast iron pot; still, if the smelter adds more limestone than is needed he is simply passing through the furnace more material than he should for the same produce of iron, thereby wasting fuel. It is here that the analytical chemist (our professor, Mr. Bentley to wit) steps in, and gives the exact quantity of fluxes for the economical smelting of the various ores the smelter is using. Very few iron ores are found to contain earthy ingredients in pro- portions sufficient to form readily fusible slags alone. Now, again, the smelter's chemist comes in and points out the necessary material. For the rich red ores of tilverston, argillaceous fluxes are necessary in addition to limestone. Some few yers ago, a substance known as "Belfast Alumi- nous Ore," containing a large amount of alumina, has come into use in the Ulverston and Whitehaven district. This piece of limestone, which I produce, I picked up at the foot of Sir William Armstrong's smelting furnaces a few months ago. It looks very like a fossilised orange. On inquiry I found it belonged to the carboniferous limestone of Harmby, Durham. Before finishing this part of my con- versation, I will give you one analysis of lime stone as chiefly used. And an analysis of the Belfast alnminous ore. The former is from the Silurian limestone, Dudley, and is used in South Staffordshire. Analysis of Calqarous Limestone.—Carbonate of lime, 9131; carbonate of Magnesia, 100; carbonate of protoxide of iron, 0132; alnmnia and protoxide of iron and silica, 1.27; organic matter, 0.20 ;water, nil.-100.40. Analysis of Belfast Alioninous Ore, by Tookey.—Silica, 915: alumina, 2195; peroxide of iron, 3591; protoxide of iron, 657 ; lime, 0 60 ; magnesia, 0 20; potash, 0 49 ; volatile 18.60.-100.12. Mr. Morris afterwards explained how the slags acted on the iron in the puddling process. The slag, or flux with scales from the finishing mills being thrown on the hearth or bottom of the furnace, how when all the iron had been melted the fluxes were the lightest, and that when the pig iron (caburet of iron) had emitted or given up its carbon to the silicates, the atoms of the iron expanded so much so that the specific gravity of the slags being the greatest had taken the place of the iron, whilst the iron had taken the form of sponge, or grains of iron knitted together. In this form the puddler shaped it into balls conveniently to take it out of the furnace for the shingler to hammer into a square bloom, for the forgo roller to pass it through the rolls to the size he was ordered to do. Mr. Morris next passed OD to describe the development of fibre from the sponge-like looking iron, assuming that the atoms or grains were cubes 1-16th of an inch in size, and that a puddled ball when hammered into a bloom one foot long they would still be the same length; when rolled into a bar 16 feet long they would then be one inch in length. These bars are cut down again fer the mill in 12 inch lengths and rolled out to 60 feet. They then become five feet long and assume the farm of fibre, and so by repeated cutting down and pilling and rolling, these fibres became as fine as silk. All iron will not develope fibre however much they might pile and roll. This was explained as well as the fact that the more the fibrous atoms were elongated the more ductile they becarne,in that direction, and the weaker the transverse way. div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Board-room, Victoria-road, on Thursday afternoon, under the presidency of Mr. T. Sutton Timmins. There were also present the Rev. Father Clarke, Messrs. R. Bradshaw, H. W. Deacon, Robert Shaw, R. H. Davies, W. Hartland, and G. H. Danby (clerk).

div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDiNCE.
div.p: SCHOOL ATTENDiNCE.

The District Education Committee reported that during the month of November (five weeks), the number of cases summoned before the committee were the following : Application for piyment of fees, 10:5 ; for controvention of Education Act, 404; total, 509. Fees were recommended to be paid in 94 cases, 41 persons were prosecuted and con- victed by the magistratPs, and one child was sent to an industrial school.—Mr. DEACON, in moving the adoption of the minutes of the committee, said there had been a great amount of sickness in the district, which accounted fer the low average, attendance at the various schools. A large number of children were suffering from measles, colds; and sore throats.—The Rev. Father CLARKE remarked that he found the attendance affected in his own schools from a similar cause. The CHAIRMAN observed that the general health of the scholars was Always affected during inclement weather, owing to the children being Insufficiently fed and clothed.—The report was adopted.

div.head: SCITOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCITOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE.

The &bool Manage- ment Committee recommended that the tender of the Garswood Coal and Iron Co, Limited, be accepted for the supply of slack and best orrel coal; and that the tender of the Widnes Local Board be accepted for the supply of coke. The committee reported that the managers of the West Bank schools had placed their resignations in the hands of the committee. They recommended that the same be accepted, and that the best thanks of the Doard be given to them for their valuable services. Mr. Davixs nsoved the confirmation of the minutes,and, referring to the resignation of the managers of West Bank Schools, said some of them had been in office since the schools were started, and he thought the best thanks of the Board were due to them for their services. They had given much time and attention, and had done their work, on the whole, very well. (Hear, hear.)—The CITAIRMLN seconded the motion, remarking that he knew something of the ;ram.; gern, and fully recognised the excellent work they had done. div.p: 'THE COST OF TEACHING.

The Finatlee rjommittee recommended accounts amount- ing to £396 As. id. for paymeut. Since the last report, £2208 15s, 3d. An elaborate tabulated statement, show- ing the 'cost ef teaching per head of children in average attendatce for the year ending August 31st, 1882, was preeftted. An analysis of the gross cost of teaching was also given. Mr. Shaw, in moving the adoption of the 'minutes, said he might congratulate the Board on the year's work of the school from a financial point of view,' and though they had not attained all they desired, they had made a considerable improvement on the previous year. He thought he might venture to say that the gradual re- ductions taking place in the cost of working the Board's schools, mainly through the exertions of the School Management Committee, was ample compensation for the trouble of collecting and bringing these figures yearly un- der the notice of the Board. The report he now submircad showed the following facts: that in what he might call the Board's best school, , Simm's Cross, the scholars In averege attendance for the school year ending August 31st, 1881, were en, and to the same date in 1882 were 788, being an increase of 95. The nett cost of teaching, or amount taken from the rate to make up the deficiency 'for this school in 1851 was £74 ISs 4d, and for 1882 £B2 14s 3d, so that the school had cost £42 4s id more during 1882 than in the year previous. (Hear, -hear.) The nett,cost per head in 1881 was 2s lid, and in 1882 ov. He considered these facts very encouraging indeed.—The Catanntoa: The school is almost self-supporting now.—Mr. SANS' (continuing) said the average attendance at Warring- on-road school in 1881 was '320, and in 1882 345, being an ncrease of 25. The amount required from the rates to
make up the difference between expenditure and income was in 1881 £179 123 id, and in 1832 £119193 9d, being

£59 12s 4d less than the preceding year. The nett cost per head in 1881 was us 2d; last year' Os 111 d, ,no that there was an improvement at that school as well. At West Bank school, the scholars in average attendance in 1881 was 714, and in 1882, 731. The nett cost of teach- ing or account taken from the rate in 1881 was £224 3s sd, and in 1882, £123 Os 7d, being a saving in the school on the year's work of £lOO 2s 10d; while the nett cost per head was in 1881, 6s 3±d, in /882, 3s 4i-d. Taking the three schools together, the total number in average attendance in 1881 was 1,727, and in 1882, 1,864; while the total nett cost of teaching in 1881 was £478 13s 10d, and in 1882 was £275 14s 7d, showing a total saving on the year's working of £202 19s 3d. He was sure they would agree with him that it was a very satisfactory report so far, but the results at each school for 1882 had only been compared with the results obtained in 1881. When the results obtained in one school were cempared with those obtained in another in similar circumstances, for the year ending August 31st, 1882, the results were not equally satisfactory. The total cost of teaching at Simm's Cross was £1.237 3s 3d, and at West Bank, £1,251 17s 10d. At Simm's Cross the average attendance was 788, and at the West Bank 731, from which they would notice that with a smaller number of scholars at West Bank there was a greater cost than at Simm's Cross. Taking the item of salaries the teachers at Simm's Cross had received, £1,092 3s 10d, and West 8ank11,062 Iss id, so that would not explain the difference. Books and apparatus at Simm's Cross had cost £54 Oa 7d, and at West Bank £BB 13s 9d. Looking at these figures it was hard to understand how, with fewer children to provide books for at the West Bank, there should be ex- pended £34 -2s at that school more than at Simm's Cross.— The CHAIRMAN suggested that the defective boiler might to some extent explain this.—Mr. SHAW thought they would be able to reduce the expense entirely. It was quite clear that there had been from some pause or other great extra- vagance in books and apparatus at West Bank foL several years, and also in one or two items, which he was sure the committee would be able to reduce.—Mr. DEACON said the receipts at each school were almost equal, and this indicated that the teaching wets pretty much on a level.—The CHAIRMAN said he had been very much interested in the report, and the thanks of the Board were due to the committee for the trouble they had taken in preparing it. Satisfactory as the figures were, he was hoping that the time would soon come when Simm's Cross and West Bank schools would be self-supporting. The attendance at schools, considering the sickness which had prevailed and inclement weather, was perfectly wonder- ful.—Mr. BRADSHAW seconded the adoption of the minutes, , which motion was carried. CHRISTMAS SHOW AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES. Christmas, accompanied with all the usual signs of en- joyment and merriment, is once again at hand. lii Runcorn and Widnes these signs are nowhere to be seen with greater brilliancy than in the windows of the tradesmen, who vie with each other in producing the most attractive show. The grocer crowds his window with a tempting array of the in- digestible ingredients of that compound which is a source of great delight to the young; the poulterer graces his boards with the denizens of the barn yard; and the butcher exhi- bits the solid fare of which Englishmen are so fond, with a fancy dressing which he attempts to prepare but once a year.
