On tae motion of Mr. JOHN' parish church of that place. He sympathized with them in their difficulties, because to his mind the state of the church at the present time was very serious indeed. They were face to face with this alternative—either to submit to be Romanised in their parish church or to be driven out. He was there to protest against that alternative, and say it ought not to be—(applause)—and they called upon the authorities in Church and State to protect the people in their proper rights and liberties—(hear, hear)—and to secure for them the worship Of Almighty God according to the doctrines as well as the formularies of the Church of England. In the name of justice it was not right that they should be driven out of their parish churches because of the Rornanising and false doctrines taught in the pulpits of some of them. As an illustration of the lamentable state of things that existed, he might say that in his church on the previous evening there was evening communion, and twelve stalwart work- ingmen for the first time presented themselves at the Lord's table to receive the memorials of His dying love at his hands. They had never been in his church before—they had been driven out of a neighbouring church because of Romanising innovations, and were compelled to take and find refuge in a church where they could get the true Gospel preached. They were there to express their sympathy with the workingmen. They had been compelled to take that action because they weredriven out from the Parish Church, because they were members of the Church Association. The Church Association was an organisation to protect the prin- ciples of the Church of England, and to prevent it being assimilated either in doctrine or worship with the Church of Rome. Was that a heinous fault? Was it a mortal sin that deserved the sentence of excom- munication? He said no. (Applause.) If it was, he deserved to be driven out of his parish church, too. He trusted the association would still adhere to its fundamental principles. If it ever altered or faltered in any way what- ever so as to interfere with the great principles of evangeli- calism which they held be would sever his connection with it altogether. He believed, however, that they would still continue to carry out the work according to the funda- mental principles they had laid down. He desired to ex- press his congratulation to them who had by God's blessing accomplished such a wonderful work as they had done. He really thought it a wonderful thing that a body of working- men without any very great social position should be able to carry out so successfully that undertaking. It was a matter of congratulation that they breathed the free Protestant spirit there—(applause)—with no note of dis- cord. They did not enter into that meeting with mutual suspicions and distrust. (Laughter.) They grasped each other's hand and recognised a brother's heart beneath. Their great aim, one and all, was to maintain those great principles that had made our country so great and above all others— principles that were essential 'to the salvation of the soul. He considered it to be their duty upon such crises as that in their church's history. Their duty in general and in that particular neighbourhood especially as Protestant churchmen was to withdraw themselves from all unhallowed association with those from whom they differed on fundamental points—(hear, hear)—to have no- thing to do with them, no amalgamation with those whom they were obliged to distrust, and with whom they had no sympathy at all; those who were preaching not a Gospel but a perversion of the true and simple Gospel of Jesus Christ. (Applause.) Protestants should organise them- selves on their own distinctive lines, and their first work was to become thoroughly acquainted with the great principles of the Reformation, and with the love of God in their hearts to maintain them. (Loud applause.) The Rev. GUSTAVUS CARSON (of Liverpool) said that on that day 193 years ago the apprentice boys of Derry closed the gates against the rebel foe and cried "No surrender," and his advice to them was "no surrender." (Applause.) He hoped they would be true to the principles they had that night met to perpetuate, and hoped and trusted that they would so spread out that before long they would have to be like the sons of the prophets and say "The place is too straight for us—give us room." Let them see after their own hearts first and in their soul know the power and love of. God, and then they could depend upon it that Christ could give them that power, that wisdom, and that protection which they needed. They must not be Protestants simply in name, but in word and in deed. They must not feel unkindly against the clergy- man of the parish—(hear, hear)—if they met him they should raise their hat as one gentleman would do to another. Let them break his heart on their knees and pray to God to bring him to a right mindedness. God had turned his enemies to be the strongest defenders of his truth, and it might be so in th it case. (Applause.) The Rev. Dr. POTTER (of Sheffield) met with a hearty reception. He said if any man came to their house preach- ing any other Gospel than that they had received they must not let him in. They might pray for the heretio and be kind to him if he needed their kindness, but they must not have anything to do with him. "There is a tide in the affairs of men," said Shakespeare, "which taken at the flood leads on to fortune," and there was a tide in the affairs of churches and of congregations of men which left it—God knew where. Many were going to the devil as fast as they could—doing the work of Satan. They had some hope of Lenesty even in a foe but they had no honesty within them. W4y were wolves in sheep's clothing with the plaintive:blest-

div.head: ST. HELENS AND THE ELECTRIC LIGHTING BILL.
div.p: ST. HELENS AND THE ELECTRIC LIGHTING BILL.

A. special meeting of the St. Helens Town Council was held in the Council Chamber, Town Hall, on Wednesday, for the purpose of rescinding the resolutions previously passed by the Council with respect to the Electric Lighting Bill. Theft were present the Mayor; Aldermen Ridley, Harrison, Cook, Mcßryde; Councillors Twyford, Jamison, Cook, Wilcock, Belsher, Gamble McKechnie, Walker, Han- son: Fisher, and Baxter.—The circular convening the meet- ing having been read, and a resolution suspending the standing orders passed, Councillor T. Coos said it might seem a little hard that the Council should be asked that day to have the resolution or resolutions passed at their last meeting rescinded so soon, but circumstances had arisen in the meantime which they considered rendered it expendient that they should do so. The Council would remember that a deputation waited on the president of the Board of Trade, and presented to him a draft provisional order, the spirit of which was that it should be permissive. The reply they received from Mr. Chamberlain they considered to be un- satisfactory and very indefinite, and therefore they thought it would be unwise at present to ask for a provisional order. He (Mr. Cook) had no doubt that in the course of the ensu- ing session some companies, and possibly some corporations, might obtain provisional orders for electric lighting, and in the meantime the Council would be able to judge from these provisional orders what were the duties and obligations which were likely to be cast on corporations in reference to the electric lighting business. They therefore thought it wisest at the present moment to stay their hands and see what the result of what these pro- visional orders should be. He might first state that the several companies who had given them notice some two or three months ago, that they intended to come into St. Helens and supply electric lighting, had not made such ap- plications, so that there was no danger of the borough being invaded by those companies during the ensuing year. The. more he had thought of that question, the more he was satis- fied that it was a serious and important one, both as to finance and to the uncertain and experimental stage at which the electric lighting.business had arrived. It seemed to be admitted on all hands that electric lighting was at present in a very experimental and tentative state, and he thought it would be unwise of that Council to seek to supply electricity to the borough of St. Helens before they knew definitely what the obligations were. He, therefore, moved that.the resolutions which had previously been passed should be rescinded.—Mr. J. C. GAMBLE seconded the pro- posal, and Alderman HARRISON, in supporting it, said he thought it would be very wise of the Council te do what the chairman of the Gas Committee proposed, considering the uncertain stage at which electric lighting bad vet reached.— I The motion was then carried unanimously, after which the ' meeting terminated.
At the Warrington Borough Court, on Monday, the license of the Prince of Wales Theatre was renewed to Mr. B. Sheridan.

How To MARE A CHRISTMAS PUDDING.—Take throe- quarters of a pound of flour, a large teaspoonful of Borwick's Gold Medal Baking Powder, two ounces of bread crumbs, a pound and a half of suet, two pounds of raisins' one pound of currants, ten ounces of sugar, two ounces of almonds, one pound of mixed candied peel, salt and spice to taste, mix ingredients well together and add six eggs well beaten, half- a-pint of old ale and one quartern of brandy. Divide in two, and Ewa eight hours.—Anvr.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
Sir Charles Dilke has been offered, and has not refused, the office of President of the Board of Trade. This ex- plains the delay in the admission of Sir C. Dilke into the Cabinet.

Yesterday a fire, which might have proved serious, was discovered in the Bankruptcy Court in the new law courts at Liverpool. Some thick beams in the floor near the fire-place were nearly burnt through when the fire was fortunately discovered.

At Wakefield yesterday, Dr. Noake, of Halton, near Leeds, and Mrs. Hudson, second-hand clothes dealer, Leeds, were remanded for a week on the charge of hav- ing murdered Margaret Scott, manageress at the Globe Tea Comprny's shop, Wakefield. . . _ .

At the Liverpool Sassions yesterday, Lewis George Wynne, assistant to a surgeon, and who bad a dispensary in Liverpool, pleaded guilty to two charges of giving false vaccination certificates, to which he signed the name of the surgeon. The prisoner was fined £5 and costs. _

Yesterday morning Mr. Moleaworth held an inquiry at Heywood into the death of Sarah Ann Dearden, nine years of age, alleged to have died through being struck with a snowball, and whose body was interred without a public inquiry. The coroner said the certificate of death given by Dr. 'Warsley was misleading, and he would report the matter to the Registrar-General, who would deal with the question. A verdict of death from being struck with a snowball was returded. •

div.head: POACHERS IN TROUBLE.
div.p: POACHERS IN TROUBLE.

John Bailey Briggs, a labourer, and WM. Blezard, a spinner, were charged at Clitheroe, yesterday, with night poaching. On Thursday night two constables saw the prisoners coming away from a plantation, and pursued them' and after an exciting chase the prisoners were cap- tured. They were ordered to pay £2 17s. each, and were also bound over.

div.head: DARING HIGHWAY ROBBERY.
div.p: DARING HIGHWAY ROBBERY.

Four men named Hayes, Jones, Svvinley, and George, were charged at Flint, on Thursday afternoon, with high- way robbery with violence.—Thomas Highlands said on Sunday night be was walking from Northop to Flint, when the prisoners sprang upon him, brutally beat him about the head arid body, and then stole his watch and chain. Pro- secutor's face still bore the marks of the affray. The prisoners, with the exception of Haves, were committed to take their trial at the Flintshire assizes. AN ANCIENT CANDIDATE FOR LIFE INSURANCE.

An extraordinary applicant recently appeared at the local office, at Bedwortb, of an insurance company, in the person of an old lady in her ninety-fifth year, who said she had come to the conclusion that it was time she was insured. The agent sent the proposal to the company, and, it appear- ing that the fair one is cheerful, active, an likely to live some time, they have undertaken the risk.

THE INTENDED PROSECUTION OF MR. BIGGAR, A Dublin correspondent telegraphs :—The Irish Govern- ment have decided to prosecute Mr. Biggar, M.P., for the speech delivered at Waterford, on Tuesday night, in which he denounced the Lord-Lieutenant as " a blood- thirsty peer; who was satisfied as to the innocence of Fran- cis Hynes and Myles Joyce when he hanged them, and sacrificed them to gratify the Whig party." On the same occasion Mr. Biggar denounced Judge. O'Brien.

div.head: WAR ALARMS.
div.p: THE WAR ALARMS.

The independent Austrian Prim and all the Hungarian papers warn Austria that the alliance with Germany is in danger, and that friendship with Russia would be most hazardous. The Hungarian papers declare unanimously that Hungary will never sanction a league of the three Emperors. The Pester Lloyd thinks it impossible that Vienna Policy should contemplate so false a step as friend- ship with Russia would be.

ELECTION OF CORONER. To awn FREEHOLDERS OF THE WEST DERBY DIVISION. MY LORDS AND GENTLEMEN. A vacancy has oocurred in the Coronership of your Division, by reason of the resignation of Mr. C. E. Driffield ; and I understand that at the Court of Freekolders, convened for Tuesday next, I am to be put in nomination as a candidate. I have practised as a Solicitor in the Borougk of St. Helens within your Division for between eight and nine years, and am, therefore; well known to a considerable section of Voters in this Election. During that period I have, of course, from time to time appeared in my professional capacity before the late Coroner and his Deputy, and still more frequently in im- portant cases before Magistrates and County Court Judges and Juries ; and have, in these and other ways, become sufficiently familiar with the laws of evidence and the conduct of judicial investigations. By far the larger number of coroner's inquests in this divisi in take place in St. Helens and the neighbouring manufacturing towns of Warrington Widnes, and Earlestown; and I submit it to you as a matter of high importance, that whoever is now to be elected should reside near one of these towns. St. Helens is not only a natural centre for the places just mentioned, bet is also within easy reach of every other district of the division; if elected. I should continue to reside there; and, apart from all other considerations, it may be pointed out that a consider- able saving to the county, in the matter of the coroner's mile- age, would result from such an arrangement. I have long had a deep conviction that, except where un- avoidable, icquests should not be held at public-houses. Not only have pubhcans themselves no interest in the continuance of the opposite system (so long existing in this division) but there are grave considerations of public convenience and social propriety arrayed against it. 1 am also of opinion that more willing publicity should be given to the proceedings of the Coroner's Court; and that every facility should be afforded to those atteading its sittings, either as friends of a deceased person or on behalf of other I affected interests, to extract the full circumstances of each fatality, and as ertain the attendant liabilities. On the above points I should, if sunessful in my candidature, endeavour to shape my practice in accordance with my theories ; and 1 trust that tb.. r-Aspeot of these possible Reforms may accuse e, at all events, a large and intelligent vote. The Polling is fixed for Thursday next. the 28th instant, at Ormskirk ; and, although this arrangement must prove fricon- venient to the large bulk of the Electors, I earnestly trust it may not deter them from asserting their franchise. Every owner of a freehold in any part of the County. no matter how small its value, provided such owner resides in the West Derby Division. is entitled to one of the Votes which I am now soliciting. Below is a list of a few of the persons who have already seen and approve of this address: and I beg to subscribe myself, My Lords and Gentlemen, Your most obedient servant. KY. COUNTY PALATINE OF LANCASTER. ELECTION 08' CORONER. TO THE FREEHOLDERS OF THE WEST DERBY DIVISION OF THE COUNTY OF LANCASTER. GENTLEMEN,— The Coronership for the above Division of the County having become vacant by the re-ignation of Charles Edward Driffield, Esquire, the late Coroner, I beg most respectfully to offer myself as a Candidate for the appointment. For a period of nearly seven years I have had the honour of being Deputy Coroner for the above Division, and for the last three or tour years, owing to the ill-health of the Coroner, the duties of the office have very largely devolved upon me. The number of Inquests held by me, since I have been Deputy Coroner, considerably exceeds 1,000, including many important enquiries, amongst them being the disastrous Railway Collision at Burscough Junction, near Ormskirk, and several Colliery Explosions; the most recent being tbe lamentable one at Abram, near Wigan, in which 48 persons were killed and several injured The inquiry occupied sine days, no less than eighty witnesses being examined, the Home Office being repre- sented by Couccil specially retained. I trust that those painful and onerous duties were satisfac- torily discharged, but of this I must leave you and the public generalry to judge. I can only add that should you honour me by electing me as successor to a Coroner who for a period of upwards ot thirty years has faithfully discharged his trust, no effort shall be wanting on my part in the endeavour to follow my p-edecessor's good example, and to merit the confidence reposed in me by the Freeholders of this Division of the County. I annex a list of the Noblemen and Gentlemen who have kindly promised me their support. Respectfully soliciting your vote and interest, I am, Gentlemen, Your obedient servant, T. W. BARKER.
